Findings for the next agent:

- **Harness locale fault (R57).** `owned-chrome.mjs` `identity()` parses
  `/bin/ps -o lstart=` with a US-order regex and runs raw `ps` on M4. macOS
  `ssh` forwards `LANG`; with `en_GB.UTF-8` M4 prints `Mon 19 Oct …` and the
  endpoint throws before writing any receipt. Launch qualifier drivers with
  `LANG=en_US.UTF-8` and no `LC_*` overrides (verified on M4). A code fix such
  as pinning `LC_ALL=C` for that `execFile` would change frozen pins and needs
  its own review cycle. R57's leftover M4 stage was removed by Root after
  identity, nonce and live-process checks, not by an independent review.
- **Setup slowdown (R58).** R54 on `3515d5b` started all 14 roles in 35 s;
  R58 took 80.6 s and R59 71.5 s. The observer runs on M4, so M1 load cannot
  slow the M4-only viewer phase. Per viewer, page creation and load took about
  1 s in R54 against 2 to 8 s in R58 and 2 to 6 s in R59; click to ready rose
  similarly. The setup read pass stayed under 0.7 s, control request rates are
  unchanged, Till was idle and sent less than in R54, and the new playlist
  retry acts only on failed loads. Earlier "2 to 4 times slower" figures were
  per-role maxima; netlog medians for R58 were 1.2 to 1.6 times R54.
- **Network environment (R59 path monitor).** M1 and M4 both use Wi-Fi and
  route all default traffic through a full-tunnel VPN. During R59,
  M4's TCP connect median to the pilot rose from 38 ms to 94 ms in setup and
  101 ms in measurement (90th percentile about 240 ms), then returned to 37 ms
  after the run; M1 rose from 40 ms to 54 ms. This was measured on one run and
  is consistent with the run's own traffic congesting the path, mostly on M4,
  which hosts 11 browsers. Relay-only TURN over TLS/TCP sends peer traffic
  between browsers on the same host out through the VPN and back. Changing the
  VPN or wiring is the user's decision; launch gates and the external path
  monitor are recorded in the R59 authorisation and result.
- **Both-quality receiver gate (R54, R59).** Contributors served for the whole
  window without budget limits, but R59 uploaded 182 MB against 15.4 MB of
  verified peer receipt. Against R54, receivers had far more expired waits
  (38 to 54 against mostly 10 or fewer), more no-budget decisions and fewer
  segments obtained after waiting. R43 on `7d7f676` had similar expired waits
  and passed, so these counts do not decide the gate.
- **The gate is marginal on every complete run.** It passed in 2 of 9 runs
  that completed measurement (R16, R43); R43 and R50 ran the same source and
  split. Receivers got 1 to 59 of about 170 segments from peers, and all
  viewers 1.7 to 5.5 per cent of bytes. Per-request records show completed
  high-quality transfers at 4 to 7 Mbit/s in 0.9 to 1.4 s, but most requests
  start with only 0.6 to 1.0 s left of a budget capped at 1.5 s
  (`originFallbackMs`; the demo does not override it), because a holder must
  first fetch the segment from origin. No high request starting with under
  900 ms left completed (0 of 217 in R54 and R59). A timed-out response still
  arrives in full, since the link protocol has no cancel: in R59 about 155 MB
  of the 167 MB of unused upload was abandoned responses, sharing the uplink
  and relay with useful transfers. Receiver 3 started high and had no high
  peer segment in its first 150 s, so this is not a switch-timing artefact.
  A network change can shift the odds but not make high-quality peer delivery
  reliable. Levers and costs, including a read-only UDP probe of the relay:
  `artifacts/both-quality-peer-gate-diagnosis-46494d5-20261019.json`.
- **Peer request floor, local commit `5ae817d`, not pushed.** Peer selection
  keeps the sizes and payload rates of the last 16 completed transfers on any
  link; the loader goes to origin, counting `segments.peerSkippedLate`, when
  the time left is below what the fastest completion at least as large would
  need for the committed size. Smaller completions never limit a larger
  request, since a low-only history would otherwise block every first
  high-quality request; without such a completion there is no limit. It stops
  requests that could not finish and their wasted upload. It gives high
  transfers no more time, so a requalification on this source alone would
  most likely still fail the both-quality gate; any gain from less congestion
  is unproved. On M4 the swarm suite passed 178 of 178, and Chrome playback
  and the account journey passed (the first version also passed all four
  operator cases); a mutation check showed the loader test depends on the
  floor. A demo cap of 3000 ms for `originFallbackMs` was tried and dropped:
  it stopped peer delivery in the loopback account-budget journey twice, for
  a reason not identified, while the floor alone passed. The qualifier
  projection does not record `peerSkippedLate`. A new source needs CI,
  deployment, the deployment review, P05, P07 and a rebuilt qualifier before
  any field result. Evidence:
  `artifacts/peer-floor-91357aa-local-tests-20261019/SUMMARY.json`.
- **Cancel and smaller send buffer, local branch `fix/peer-cancel`, not
  pushed.** Two commits on `5ae817d`, made in a scratch worktree:
  `51d992d` (a receiver that starts draining sends `{"t":"cancel","id":n}`; a
  holder declines with `none` before `meta` or stops at its next chunk and
  sends EOF early; a short EOF is accepted only after sending cancel; holders
  count `bytes.uploadsCancelled` and `bytes.uploadCancelledBytes`, with no
  refund of charged allowance; `docs/NIP-DRAFT.md` and `INTEGRATION.md`
  updated) and `4178c26` (a holder queues more only while at most 128 KiB is
  waiting, resuming at 32 KiB, instead of 1 MiB and 256 KiB; without this a
  670 KB high segment was queued in one pass and a cancel had nothing left to
  stop). The Swift kit (`relayswarm-kit` 2f0b26a) is receive-only and never
  serves, drains or cancels. On M4 all suites passed, including real-Chrome
  peer-first with no loss of peer share; loopback peers never timed out, so
  cancel itself is proved only by unit and loader tests. Mutation checks
  covered each path. The qualifier observer records only `totals.uploaded`;
  measuring the saving in the field needs the rebuilt qualifier to keep
  `bytes.uploadCancelledBytes`. Evidence:
  `artifacts/peer-cancel-4178c26-local-tests-20261019/SUMMARY.json`.

  **Read-only diagnosis (`artifacts/r61-throughput-diagnosis-20261019/DIAGNOSIS.json`),
  corrected by the structural analysis below.** Holder links peaked at
  3.9 Mbit/s (R60 15.2, R59 9.1) and no high-quality request ran faster than
  2.75 Mbit/s (R60 5.17). Cancelled responses keep their charge against the
  512 000 B/s upload token bucket, so the busiest holder refused 137 requests
  (R60: 7) after 77 MB of charged bytes were never sent. The first version
  said the environment did not explain the drop and led with the 128 KiB
  send buffer; both are corrected below.
  The concurrent session on this Mac is working on Spotlight
  indexing, which explains much of M1's load.
  **Structural analysis
  (`artifacts/high-quality-peer-structure-analysis-20261019/ANALYSIS.json`,
  read-only, R59 to R61).** Findings:
  - *Playback regression in R61.* Every peer-first viewer at high quality
    stalled: receivers 5 to 8 times (7 to 14 s), high contributors 9 to 15
    times on 3 of 4. Origin-only baselines barely stalled; R60 had almost
    none. The frame/audio gate still passed. The stalls followed quality and
    peer-first mode, not host: low-quality contributors on M4 stalled once
    or twice for under a second. That points to the high-quality wait loop
    rather than the path alone, but the records cannot separate 4178c26
    from the slower path.
  - *The 1.5 s cap, not playback, bounded R60.* At high-quality decisions,
    R60 receivers had a median 7.9 s of buffer. With the 2 s origin reserve
    kept, 87% could have waited at least 3.5 s. In R61 the high buffer had
    collapsed to 3.5 s, so the cap bound only about 15% of decisions there.
  - *A high segment needs far more than 1.5 s.* About 0.7 s goes on waiting
    for a holder (budget left at request p50 739 to 783 ms). Typical requests
    then ramp the same way in R60 and R61, gaining about 0.37 of a segment
    per second after a slow start. A whole segment needs roughly 2.5 to 3 s
    from the request. The smaller send buffer lowered the fastest links but
    not the typical request, so it is one unproved contributor, not the
    lead cause.
  - *The environment was worse in R61, contrary to the first diagnosis.*
    High-quality HTTP fetches by peer-first roles were 40 to 65% slower on
    3 of 4 high contributors; low-quality fetches were unchanged. Both runs
    were without the VPN. Origin timing per request was not recorded, so path
    capacity and self-inflicted fallback bursts cannot be separated.
  - *Likely feedback loop (inferred).* A failed high wait costs up to 1.5 s
    plus the HTTP fetch, close to the 2 s segment in R60 and over it in R61.
    The buffer then drains toward the reserve, the budget shrinks toward
    zero, and requests start with little time left. R61 had 96 high requests
    given under 400 ms (p50 25 ms), 91 of which received nothing. The code
    charges each accepted request a whole segment before sending. Records
    carry no holder id, and the timing correlation with refusals (0.38) is
    no stronger than for other timeouts, so the size of this drain is
    unproved.
  - *Gate arithmetic.* Each receiver needs one verified high peer segment in
    about 150 s at high (about 60 attempts). A 5% per-attempt completion
    rate gives about 95% per receiver; R60 managed 1%, R59 4%, R61 0%.
  - *Projection.* From each timeout's own partial rate (pessimistic), a cap
    of 3 to 5 s would let 18 to 32% of R60's high timeouts finish, but only
    where the buffer allows it.
  - *Receiver 2 in R61.* It had four links and no dial or admission
    failures; its only peer segment arrived before measurement.
  - *Loopback cap failure.* The 3000 ms cap failure in the loopback journey
    is still unexplained.
  - *Process.* Floor, cancel and the smaller buffer were each proved only
    on loopback, where peers never time out. No local bench reproduces a
    160 to 200 ms relayed round trip.
  The analysis lists the levers and their costs: wait cap, request floor,
  charge semantics, early give-up, buffer depth, segment size, send buffer,
  UDP relay addresses and cut-through sending.

  limit (low quality 1.5 Mbit/s, R64 1.2), timed from request, so first-byte
  delay is included. The limiter is one token bucket per contributor with a
  two-second burst, shared across its links, and a holder queues at most
  128 KiB (since `4178c26`). M4's Wi-Fi took in 3.22 MB/s during R65's
  measurement and 3.17 MB/s in R64's. All 48 links open at the end of R65
  were relay to relay over TLS, as the recorded relay-only profile requires,
  so every peer byte went to Till and back over TLS/TCP. The round trip to
  the TURN service was about 84 ms from M1 and 102 ms from M4, roughly 170
  to 200 ms per link. That path is the leading candidate, not yet tested.
  The high rendition is about 2.6 Mbit/s, so a single high-quality peer
  transfer at the observed median runs slower than real time. Addendum:
  `artifacts/distributed-fourteen-qualifier-5f2ece0-r65-result-addendum-20261020.json`.
  Cleanup passed on M1, M4 and Till, the live app `8534fff7` is unchanged,
  and the docs stash was restored with matching checksums. Record:
  `artifacts/distributed-fourteen-qualifier-5f2ece0-r65-result-20261020.json`.
  Awaiting the user's decision.
- **UDP relay addresses, not chosen.** The relay answered a STUN binding over
  UDP 3478 from M4; the demo already supports `--turn-url-projection issued`,
  still relay-only, but that changes the recorded pilot profile and requires
  fresh Apply and upload consent, so it is the user's decision.
- **Local link bench (20 October, 19:10 to 21:24 UTC, local only, no host
  action; its TCP figure is overstated, see the field probe below).** The user asked to test
  the transfer rate at about 200 ms locally. Two headless Chrome pages ran
  the 5f2ece0 PeerLink. Chrome DevTools latency proved lossy (6 to 8% of
  peer packets), so delay came from a counted UDP relay on loopback. At a
  196.5 ms round trip with no loss, a high segment ran at 6.5 Mbit/s and a
  low one at 2.8 Mbit/s, about 1.0 s and 0.6 s from the request. The
  pre-4178c26 1 MiB queue reached 8.9 Mbit/s on high segments (1 of 3 runs
  valid; the others lost packets on loopback). Through a local coturn of
  Till's image (`coturn/coturn:4.17.2-r0`) at 197 ms, TURN over TCP ran at
  1.0 Mbit/s in two checks, with 35 and 39 packets lost and none in netem
  or Chrome; a third check's link failed with a channel error. coturn's
  source drops relayed data bound for a TCP/TLS client, without counting or
  logging it, once 32 KiB is queued (always on), and every R65 link went
  through a coturn TLS leg. TURN over UDP reached 3.3 Mbit/s, a lower
  bound, because that cell lost 3.5% between Docker's UDP forwarding and
  coturn. A UDP relay avoids the drop rule but not field loss: 1% seeded
  loss alone gave 0.6 Mbit/s, then the holder's 3 s drain deadline closed
  the link. The pilot's `tls-tcp` projection keeps only the issued TLS
  address; `issued` keeps UDP, TCP and TLS, so a browser would use UDP where
  it works. R65's records also show (inferred, no holder identity recorded)
  receiver-1 waiting on a same-quality link that was never ahead, with
  neighbour discovery making no checks, while receivers 2 and 4 got haves
  but no high transfer fitted their budget. Record:
  `artifacts/link-throughput-bench-20261020/FINDINGS.md`. Awaiting the
  user's decision.
- **Field probe: one TLS relay link through Till runs at 3 to 4 Mbit/s, and
  UDP relay does not help (20 October, 21:38 to 22:19 UTC).** The user
  approved the single-link probe ("do it"). Holder Chrome on M1, receiver
  Chrome on M4 in a fresh profile over SSH, relay-only through the shared
  TURN service with one issued URL per cell, both Macs on Wi-Fi with no
  tunnel, one fresh issuer credential per repetition (values not recorded,
  files deleted). Nothing in the pilot, consent or Till changed. A high
  segment ran at a median 3.15 and 3.8 Mbit/s over TLS and 4.2 and
  3.35 Mbit/s over TCP, 18 of 18 requests each, losing 0.2 to 0.6%. UDP ran
  at 3.35 Mbit/s with 1.6% loss; in a second cell the holder's 3 s drain
  deadline closed the link after 7 of 18 requests, and the smoke check lost
  7.7%. The path was jittery (ping spread 64 to 149 ms) and background
  traffic was not controlled; M4's load reached 70 from the owner's work in
  one cell. Two repetitions completed; a third and a first attempt stopped
  at the M1 quiet gate. So R65's 2.1 Mbit/s comes from what the qualifier
  adds (concurrent uploads sharing the house uplink, 11 roles on M4's
  Wi-Fi, admission, loss under load), not from one TLS link, and switching
  to UDP relay addresses is not supported. Cleanup proved on both Macs.
  Record: `artifacts/link-throughput-bench-20261020/FINDINGS.md`. Awaiting
  the user's decision.
- **v0.2.0 published as an experimental GitHub prerelease (21 October,
  about 00:25 UTC).** The user said "commit push merge ship" and chose a
  v0.2.0 prerelease. The handover docs and a release-preparation docs commit
  (`fd046f5`) passed all nine required CI jobs; PR 8 merged as `bf43940`
  (merge commit, tree identical to `fd046f5`), whose main CI run 39514327948
  also passed. Annotated tag `v0.2.0` points to `bf43940`. Assets (tarball,
  standalone bundle, `SHA256SUMS`) were built from a clean archive with the
  recipe that rebuilds v0.1.0's bundle byte for byte, then downloaded from the
  public URLs and verified; see [Status](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md#release-verification).
  Field gates stay open: the qualifier is RED and the pilot still runs
  `5f2ece0` without the release's clock-skew diagnostics. No npm publish.
- **R60 is RED on the same single gate (19 October, 15:34 to 15:40 UTC).**
  Source 46494d5, Till app 124e3bcc unrestarted, 3 roles on M1 and 11 on M4,
  302 s measured, both Macs on the LAN with no VPN carrying the default route.
  15 of 16 gates passed; `each4BothQualityPeer` failed (only receiver 2 had
  both qualities from peers). 3 of 309 high-quality peer requests completed,
  none of the 236 that started with under 1100 ms left; 14.2 MB verified peer
  media against 189 MB uploaded. Removing the VPN did not rescue the gate on
  this source. Launch deviation: R59's M4 connect bound (45 ms) was set on the
  VPN path; without it both Macs connect in a steady 57 to 71 ms, so the launch
  used that baseline, recorded in the authorisation. The checkout was detached
  at 46494d5 for the run and restored (checksums matched). Cleanup confirmed on
  M1, M4 and Till; the Till control directory keeps its journal like R57 to
  R59. The app health check fails whenever no source is publishing, which is
  idle state between runs. Result:
  `artifacts/distributed-fourteen-qualifier-46494d5-r60-result-20261019.json`.
- R58 and R59 cleanup were confirmed by Root fresh read-only checks on M1, M4
  and Till; the formal independent cleanup review method (R55 lineage) was not
  rebased.
- Scope: steps 1 to 3 used one M1 Chrome against the live pilot over the real
  network. They do not test multi-viewer peer delivery (P01).

Findings for the next agent:

- **R66 was run at the R65 profile** (contributors at 1,250,000 B/s, four
  neighbours, relay-only TURN over TLS/TCP, no VPN tunnel on either Mac, checked
  by the authorisation) on the rebuilt source. It is a short desktop-class
  result; it says nothing about 7,200 s, devices or a separate network.
- **TURN is a separate host from the origin.** The origin served about 226 MB
  less than all-origin delivery over R66's 302 s window, but total egress across
  both hosts rose by roughly 85 to 100 MB. Do not describe this as a bill
  saving: the hosts' plan terms are not recorded.
- **R38's rejoin race is a harness fault.** `rejoin()` in the long lineage reads
  the actor straight after clicking Start; the page applies settings
  asynchronously. A fix needs its own review cycle and a new run. No earlier long
  run reached a rejoin, so the rejoin itself has no evidence either way.
- **P06's role summary fields do not update.** Do not cite `videoQualities`,
  `verifiedPeerQualities`, `zeroFrameIntervals` or `contributionWithdrawn` for
  P06 or a416f7e; the observer never assigns `measurementStarted`. Use the raw
  samples.
- **P06 is a design limitation, not a product defect.** The shared allowance
  behaved as documented in [Account upload budget](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/ACCOUNT-UPLOAD-BUDGET.md).
  About 660 KB high-quality segments did not complete within the receiver's
  buffer-safe wait on the relay path (about 255 KB/s on the best link), so three
  accepted reservations consumed the cap before the fourth was refused.
- **P06 at 6 MB stops on the page's own cap.** Each uploading page snapshots the
  smaller of its local allowance and the account's remaining allowance when
  uploading is applied (`demo/client.mjs`) and refuses locally with
  `session-allowance` before any account reservation once a segment exceeds its
  own remainder (`src/browser/hls-swarm.mjs`). The account refusal the stage
  waits for can only come from a donor whose local remainder lies within the
  other devices' spend of one segment; at 6 MB that window was narrower than one
  720p segment, so no cap size reaches it in this scenario. Two product findings
  follow: a holder keeps advertising segments it will always refuse, because
  serving stops only at exactly zero remaining, and the receiver has no back-off
  against a holder that refuses every request (39 wasted round trips); and the
  page cap is never refreshed from the account after it is applied. Fixing
  either is a product cycle.
- **R68's both-quality failure is a product mechanism on a one-segment margin.**
  Receivers switch quality together about 150 s in. In R66 receiver-1 received
  exactly one high-quality peer segment after switching, so R66 passed by one
  segment. In R68, with origin media fetches 1.5 to 2 times slower (cause not
  determined; the pilot server and small control requests were unchanged),
  receivers 1 and 2 received none. The projection in `src/browser/hls-swarm.mjs`
  declines a peer request when the holder wait plus first byte exceeds the room
  left; the holder wait is the viewer's own origin median, so each fallback
  raises the next estimate, and there is no back-off. With no high-quality
  holder ahead, HAVE waits expire; transfers of about 670 KB over the relay are
  abandoned at the deadline; and a spent neighbour replacement resets only on a
  verified high-quality segment (`src/browser/neighbour-discovery.mjs`). These
  are findings, not fixes. Holder labels carry no mapping to roles, and the
  origin-only baselines record no origin latency, so the evidence cannot say
  which contributor served whom.
- **Identity rebases miss bare hash pins.** R67's generator re-pinned path
  records from the archive but copied `dependency-pins.json` `lockSHA256`, which
  the controller checks against the checkout. R68's generator refuses stale
  hashes of changed runtime files, and its authorisation runs the controller's
  own dependency check first.
- **Decisions.** The user chose to record Item 5 and P06 as RED and open and to
  move on. After one 6 MB run on `1d54538`, the user chose to stop P06. After
  R67 stopped on the harness pin, the user chose R68; after R68 was RED, the user
  chose to record Item 5 RED and stop it.

Prepared review/test directories include their own README, manifests and bounds.
Read them before execution. Null future results or synthetic pure-test inputs
are not live proof. Use current provenance and private input pins; do not run an
old bound command against a replacement container.

## Working constraints and reporting

- Other jobs on M1/M4 must keep running. Do not kill unrelated processes, ask the
  owner to pause their work, or raise resource/process limits to make tests pass.
- The physical iPhone is currently unavailable. Continue independent work and
  leave that acceptance item explicitly open; do not repeat unlock/cable requests.
- Preserve explicit upload/reporting consent, spent quota, private publisher and
  account state, permanent lease inodes, and the independent router/proxy.
- The recorded pilot uses relay-only TLS/TCP TURN through the existing service,
  admission address limits of 32 tickets and 900 requests, and four demo
  neighbours. The SDK default remains six. Recheck the runtime contract rather
  than silently changing this profile or treating it as six-neighbour capacity.
- Restore any test-owned temporary privacy, reporting or network changes. Stop
  owned fixtures/browsers/emulators and remove owned scratch after retaining
  evidence. Leave the permanent pilot/router/proxy running intentionally.
- Keep the original acceptance windows and cleanup reserves. Failure or resource
  pressure calls for diagnosis, not relaxed requirements or erased fatal records.
- Preserve supported-media boundaries. A custom ABR engine, DRM/SAMPLE-AES,
  durable media storage and an accepted RelaySwarm NIP are not existing features.
- Report each result with source, runtime, topology/device, duration, verdict,
  evidence path and cleanup. Separate implementation, local tests, CI, deployment,
  physical acceptance and publication. Report actual progress and remaining gates
  plainly; do not present another preparation pass as completed field acceptance.

Start with `git status --short --branch`, refresh `origin`, and confirm the PR
head before relying on this snapshot. For documentation edits, update authored
Markdown and `llms.txt`, then run `npm run docs:generate` and
`npm run check:docs`. Node 22.13+ is required; CI uses Node 24. Preserve all
unrelated work and follow the repository's resource-cleanup instructions.

Source: [docs/BROADCASTING.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/BROADCASTING.md)

# Broadcaster source workflow

[Documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/README.md) · [Operations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/OPERATIONS.md) · [Container deployment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/deploy/README.md) · [Evidence](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md)

This guide describes the v0.2.1 broadcaster workflow, persistent publisher state and operator/reporting controls. Install [v0.2.1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/GETTING-STARTED.md); the immutable v0.1.0 assets do not include these additions. Publication of a guide does not establish deployed playback or platform acceptance.

## Local source and dependencies

Use Node 24 and ffmpeg with libx264 and AAC. RTMPS input/forwarding additionally requires a DNS hostname and FFmpeg major version 5 or later built with GnuTLS, or major version 8 or later built with OpenSSL. Install the source dependencies and the pinned MediaMTX router:

```sh
npm ci
npm run broadcast:install
```

The installer downloads MediaMTX 1.21.2 for macOS/Linux x64 or arm64, checks the archive against a platform-specific pinned SHA-256 before extraction, and prints the executable path. Its owner-controlled cache is `artifacts/tools/mediamtx-v1.21.2`; a private receipt records the extracted binary digest. A cached receipt is trusted local state, not independent upstream attestation. On another platform supply your own compatible router executable.

Start the bundled local router and broadcaster from the repository root:

```sh
npm run broadcast -- \
  --mediamtx artifacts/tools/mediamtx-v1.21.2/mediamtx \
  --state-dir artifacts/broadcast
```

Configure OBS Custom streaming with server `rtmp://127.0.0.1:1935/live` and an empty stream key. Supply **both H.264 video and AAC audio**. The bundled router listens only on loopback, refuses a second publisher for `live`, and exposes its RTSP read path at `rtsp://127.0.0.1:8554/live`. The launcher reads that path over TCP. Without `--mediamtx`, run the router separately or provide `--input` for an existing supported network source. Supported input schemes are RTSP, RTMP, RTMPS and SRT. RTSPS is rejected because verified TLS behaviour is not portable across supported FFmpeg versions; scheme acceptance does not prove compatibility with every source.

The launcher first binds a waiting listener and prints its address, normally `http://localhost:8787`. The root page returns HTTP 200 and checks again every three seconds. Before both HLS renditions publish, other endpoints return bounded HTTP 503 responses with `Retry-After: 3`; there is no session, relay or operator API on the waiting listener. Once output is ready, the launcher replaces that listener with the player on the same port. A waiting page proves HTTP availability, not media playback. Stop with Ctrl-C for orderly listener, worker and router shutdown.

An external OBS workstation can use an authorised SSH tunnel rather than a public plaintext RTMP listener:

```sh
ssh -N -L 1935:127.0.0.1:1935 deploy@your-host
```

OBS then targets its own loopback address. The container router uses an internal app/router network plus a separate normal bridge needed for its loopback RTMP port publication; RTSP has no published host port. Container ingest mappings and the existing/new HTTPS proxy choices are in the [deployment guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/deploy/README.md). Remote browsers require configured TLS or an explicit `--public-url https://your-hostname` behind an HTTPS proxy. The public origin must match browser Origin headers. Configure repeated `--relay wss://...` options if using external relays; otherwise the server supplies its own bounded relay at `/relay`. `--stun` accepts a STUN URL. Alternatively, `--ice-config FILE` loads private host-provided STUN/TURN browser credentials; the [field guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/FIELD-TEST.md#use-separate-devices-and-networks) gives the bounded format and disclosure boundary. No TURN deployment is supplied.

For an existing short-lived credential issuer, use
`--turn-credentials-url https://issuer.example/turn` instead of `--stun` or
`--ice-config`. The optional [renewal adapter](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/FIELD-TEST.md#optional-turn-credential-renewal)
is off by default. It obtains separate viewer credentials, refreshes active
peer sessions and retains consent and spent allowances. It supplies no TURN
deployment; expired credentials leave playback on origin until fresh Apply.

Admission defaults to 12 tickets per minute for each socket address. Viewers
behind a reverse proxy can share that address. Set
`--admission-per-address-tickets 32` when the operator intends that capacity;
accepted values are integers 1–120, default 12. The launcher validates the value
before creating state or starting services. This changes no global issuance,
request, expiry or consent limit, and does not trust forwarded-address headers.
Choosing a limit does not establish a passing multi-viewer qualification.

Admission also defaults to 600 requests per minute for each socket address,
shared by challenge, ticket and verification requests. Configure
`--admission-per-address-requests 900` only when the operator intends that
allowance; accepted values are integers 1–10,000, default 600. Validation runs
before state creation or service startup. Behind Caddy or another reverse proxy,
viewers can share one backend socket address; forwarded-address headers remain
untrusted. The global request limit remains 2,048 per minute, global ticket
issuance remains 120 per minute, and all other admission limits remain unchanged.
The pilot plans an explicit 900 after observing 637 startup admission requests
within a minute, allowing headroom over that observation. This setting has not
yet been deployed or qualified; configuring it does not prove field capacity or
resolve the separate delayed-response observations.

The broadcaster and demo accept `--ice-transport-policy all|relay`, default
`all`. Choose `relay` explicitly to restrict peer ICE to relayed candidates;
provide usable TURN configuration or the existing credential adapter. The
choice does not force TLS: by default the adapter preserves all validated issuer
URLs. It never falls back to `all`, changes the peer deadline or grants upload
consent. Playback keeps its existing origin fallback. A changed demo session
policy stops peers and requires fresh Apply and upload consent. This option
does not establish improved delivery, measured privacy or field acceptance.

With the optional credential issuer, `--turn-url-projection tls-tcp` selects
secure TCP configuration independently of the ICE candidate policy. Default
`issued` preserves the existing descriptor and issued URLs. The adapter retains
its original raw cache/lease, preserves explicit secure TCP URLs, and appends
`?transport=tcp` only where a valid `turns:` URI left transport unspecified.
It excludes plain TURN and explicit UDP; it changes no host, port, credentials,
issuer TTL or refresh boundary. The client enforces the projected response too.
No supported result means origin fallback, never unrestricted retry. Changing
selection stops peers and requires fresh Apply/upload consent. This is an
application-selected URI, not the unchanged issuer response or a capability
proof; see the [API contract and primary standards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/API.md#optional-tls-over-tcp-url-projection).
No existing issuer/service configuration is changed by this option.

## Output and recovery

Add `--account-budget` to offer the optional shared upload allowance. It keeps
`account-budget.json` in the private state directory and supports explicit
Nostr sign-in. Website account authentication uses the JavaScript host callback,
not a viewer-supplied account identifier. The Compose template enables the
offer through `ACCOUNT_BUDGET_ENABLED=1`; viewers still choose whether to connect
an account and separately opt into uploading. Preserve the ledger and its
permanent lease files. See [shared upload allowance](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/ACCOUNT-UPLOAD-BUDGET.md).

The encoder produces two fixed H.264/AAC renditions:

| Rendition | Frame shape/rate | Target video rate | Audio |
|---|---|---|---|
| low | 640 × 360, 30 fps | 700 kbps | AAC, 128 kbps, 48 kHz stereo |
| high | 1280 × 720, 30 fps | 2,500 kbps | AAC, 128 kbps, 48 kHz stereo |

Scaling preserves aspect ratio and pads to the fixed frame shape. Each rendition uses a two-second segment target and a twelve-segment live playlist: approximately **24 seconds of listed media**, not a 120-second playlist. ffmpeg retains an additional deletion tail; prior process generations have a separate two-minute pruning grace by default. These durations are storage/publication policy, not a measured end-to-end latency guarantee. Both renditions belong to one supported codec/frame-rate family; this is a fixed ladder, not a general encoding service.

The HLS worker and optional forwarding worker retry independently, with bounded exponential delay. Each HLS process generation uses a distinct segment directory and a persisted discontinuity sequence. Variant/master publication uses atomic file replacement. A directory watch on the current generation starts publication when ffmpeg renames a playlist into place; a 250 ms interval remains the fallback. Source loss leaves the last published playlists available while workers reconnect; old HTTP availability does not establish fresh media or successful decoder recovery. Inspect publication age in operator status.

Use a dedicated canonical state directory owned by the launching user, preferably mode **0700**, with no symlink components or group/world writes. New directories use 0700. The launcher keeps `publisher.json` and `operator-token` as owner-only **0600**, regular, single-link files. The publisher file contains a private signing key and its signed redistribution authorisation; neither secret is delivered in browser sessions or operator status. Existing malformed/mismatched publisher state is rejected rather than replaced. Restarting with the same state retains publisher identity, swarm ID and authorisation; starting with another state directory creates another identity.

Only one pipeline may use a media directory. `/state/media/.broadcast-lock` in the container, or `STATE_DIR/media/.broadcast-lock` natively, is acquired exclusively. Orderly close removes it. An unclean exit may leave it and the next start fails closed. Stop all possible users of that volume/directory and establish exclusive ownership before manual stale-lock removal; never infer safety from a PID in a different namespace or delete locks automatically. See [operations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/OPERATIONS.md#restart-and-recovery).

## Optional RTMPS forwarding

Create a private, owner-controlled directory outside the checkout. In it, use a private editor to write one line containing the complete RTMPS ingest URL to a regular, single-link file owned by the launching user, mode **0600**. Keep the parent mode **0700** and use its canonical path. Start with:

```sh
npm run broadcast -- \
  --mediamtx artifacts/tools/mediamtx-v1.21.2/mediamtx \
  --state-dir artifacts/broadcast \
  --youtube-url-file /absolute/private/directory/youtube-url
```

The file supplies the URL without putting the stream key in environment variables or launcher arguments. For RTMPS input or forwarding, the pipeline first checks the selected executable’s version/build configuration with a five-second, 32 KiB output budget, before creating media state or workers. Direct callers of the argument builders must perform equivalent capability validation themselves. Forwarding has its own ffmpeg process and source reader, copies the H.264/AAC tracks into FLV, requires RTMPS, explicitly enables TLS certificate/hostname verification and sets a 15-second output I/O timeout. It does not transcode for a platform's separate compatibility rules. A forwarding outage cannot block the HLS process, although both still depend on the same source and host resources.

Trusted host/container administrators can inspect ffmpeg's process arguments, which contain the full ingest URL. The implementation consumes upstream stderr without publishing credentials in logs, metrics or browser sessions. Protect the host, secret file and process-inspection permissions accordingly. Restart the broadcaster to read a changed URL. A process marked running/connecting or repeated restarts is **not** evidence that YouTube accepted the stream or that viewers can play it; confirm that separately in an authorised platform test.

## Verification boundary

The source includes native process/publication tests and actual Chrome fixtures.
The dated [status](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md) retains the authorised OBS and private YouTube
tests; that YouTube broadcast was stopped and deleted. Current deployed `8f482b4`
playback passed its ordinary short check, while both-quality peer delivery and
the fourteen-role qualification remain red. Complete physical-device,
separate-network/hard-NAT, sustained-operation and final release acceptance
remain open. Earlier passes retain their original source and scope.

The broadcast browser fixture uses loopback Chrome, synthetic media and explicit
RTC/fake-media fixture flags. Its receipt adds bounded observations of existing
media request events: at most four pages, 512 shared object labels, 256 retained
rows and 64 tracked active requests per page. Labels correlate the same private
pathname/range within one run; they do not reveal paths, queries or parsed
playlist sequence/continuity. Fixed media/rendition categories and numeric cached
Playwright timings distinguish request start, response and completion. Unavailable
values remain null; evictions, overflow and pending requests remain explicit.
The unpopulated native epoch placeholder is null; zero remains valid for
relative timings.
Snapshots before and after browser close are separate observations. The recorder
adds no requests or body reads and changes no playback deadline or assertion.
It is diagnostic evidence, not ordinary network or physical-device qualification.

Source: [docs/CORE-PACKAGING.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/CORE-PACKAGING.md)

# Native core release packaging

The v0.4.0 release uses this workflow to prepare native core assets. It creates no tag or GitHub release,
publishes nothing to npm, and leaves `core/apple/Package.swift` using `path:`.
A binary URL dependency remains a separate release decision.

## Triggers and permissions

The existing [test workflow](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/.github/workflows/test.yml) calls
[native packaging](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/.github/workflows/core-packages.yml) on a tag push, or
when explicitly dispatched with `core_packages: true`. Ordinary branch pushes
and pull requests do not run the release-packaging jobs. Their existing
validation jobs retain their normal behaviour.

The packaging-only dispatch skips the ordinary test matrix, builds Apple and
Android artefacts, uploads them to Actions and verifies their checksums and
source commit. Build/download jobs have read-only repository permission.
The attachment job requires **both** a tag-push event and the caller's publish
flag; a dispatch cannot attach assets, including when dispatched at a tag.

On a tag push, attachment requires an already existing GitHub release for that
tag. It fails if the release does not exist, and never creates one. Uploads
omit `--clobber`, so existing release assets are not replaced. Both platforms
must build and pass the combined verification before attachment. The caller
grants write permission only to the reusable workflow; only its attachment
job uses that permission.

## Dry run

From the candidate checkout:

```sh
gh workflow run test.yml --ref <candidate-branch> -f core_packages=true
gh run view <run-id>
gh run download <run-id> --pattern 'relayswarm-core-*' --dir artifacts/core-release-download
node scripts/package-core-release.mjs verify artifacts/core-release-download
```

The entry point already exists on the default branch, so the dispatch can test
a new reusable-workflow file on an unmerged candidate branch. Use a fresh
empty download directory and check out the exact dispatched commit before
verification. The verifier rejects mismatched source commits, missing or
unexpected assets and invalid checksums. Actions artefacts are retained for
30 days; a successful dispatch is not a release or publication.

## Assets

| File | Content |
|---|---|
| `relayswarm-core.xcframework.zip` | The binary XCFramework at the archive root, arm64 for iPhone, iOS simulator and macOS |
| `relayswarm-core.xcframework.zip.checksum` | Actual `swift package compute-checksum` result for that archive |
| `relayswarm-core-swift-bindings.zip` | Handwritten Swift facade and unchanged local-path `Package.swift` |
| `relayswarm-core.aar` | Kotlin bindings and native libraries for arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a and x86_64 |
| `SHA256SUMS-apple`, `SHA256SUMS-android` | Digests of each platform's assets and metadata |
| `BUILD-METADATA-apple.json`, `BUILD-METADATA-android.json` | Source commit, package version, Node and Rust versions |

Extract both Apple archives into one directory to obtain the existing local
Swift package. Its minimums are macOS 14 and iOS 16. The build compiles the
Swift wrapper against the actual XCFramework before archiving it.
The SwiftPM checksum describes the binary archive, not the bindings archive.

The Android minimum is API 26 and consumers need Kotlin 2.2 or later; JNA is
not required. Each ABI contains Rust and JNI shared libraries. The builder
checks each library's machine, 16 KiB load alignment for 64-bit libraries and
system-library dependencies. Packaging checks the manifest, classes, consumer
rules and all six libraries.

## Local build and scope

```sh
npm ci
node scripts/package-core-release.mjs apple
node scripts/package-core-release.mjs android
node scripts/package-core-release.mjs verify
```

Apple needs macOS/Xcode and the three Rust Apple targets. Android needs the
SDK/NDK, SDK platform 36, cargo-ndk 4.1.2, Kotlin and the three Rust Android
targets, as the existing builders require. Each build uses the worktree's own
`core/target`; it sets no separate target directory or incremental policy.
Source paths are remapped for native builds and checked before archiving.
Source commits and hashes bind each platform's outputs to the same checkout.

These checks cover build/packaging and local or CI consumption. They do not
prove physical-device, mobile battery, public-NAT or field acceptance, and add
no native WebRTC adapter, client application or transport dependency.

## JavaScript and WASM downloads

From a clean release commit after `npm ci`, run `npm run release:build`.
It checks the committed WASM source stamp, audits the npm package file list,
bundles the browser loader without external imports and writes the tarball,
separate module, source metadata and `SHA256SUMS` under `artifacts/release`.
It creates no tag or release. Verify fresh consumption before uploading those
files to the same release as the source-matched native assets.

---

Source: [docs/CORE-SIGNATURE-BUDGET.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/CORE-SIGNATURE-BUDGET.md)

# Core signature verification budget

Measured 24 October 2026 at source `cd92d3690b9e32b7f5932ea0b703f42a41a13eb9`.
This is an isolated experiment; the shipping Rust, JavaScript and committed
WASM module are unchanged. The [raw measurements](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/spikes/results/core-signature-budget-20261024.json)
include asset hashes, per-round timings and tool versions.

## Recommendation

Keep signature verification in the core for now, with the WASM module served
as a separate compressed asset. Delegating checks to the already-bundled
`nostr-tools` saved about 3% of the combined compressed client/module bytes,
but the measured imported-verifier path took longer per commitment. It also
adds a host import to the currently import-free module. This result supports
retaining one verifier across browser and native targets; it does not establish
which isolated Schnorr implementation is intrinsically faster.

## Asset sizes

Both variants use the demo's minified browser ESM build, the same pinned Rust
release configuration (`opt-level=z`, LTO, no `wasm-opt`) and a separately fetched
module. Compression is gzip level 9 and Brotli quality 11. Totals sum the two
separately compressed assets; they exclude HTTP headers and cache effects.
The rebuilt baseline module is byte-identical to the committed module.

| Asset | Core checks: raw / gzip / Brotli bytes | Imported nostr-tools checks: raw / gzip / Brotli bytes |
|---|---:|---:|
| Demo client | 823,969 / 261,901 / 216,987 | 824,082 / 261,922 / 216,961 |
| WASM module | 406,612 / 150,394 / 122,190 | 369,884 / 137,844 / 112,356 |
| Combined | 1,230,581 / 412,295 / 339,177 | 1,193,966 / 399,766 / 329,317 |

The prototype saves 36,615 raw bytes, 12,529 gzip bytes or 9,860 Brotli bytes
across the pair. The client already includes `nostr-tools` for relay/session
verification; moving commitment checks does not remove it from the baseline.

## Verification time

Apple M1, macOS arm64, headless Chrome 155.0.8059.85, Node 24.21.0 for building and Rust
1.94.1, nostr-tools 2.24.1 and esbuild 0.28.2. Each variant passed all 140 shared commitment/delegation/revocation
vectors through Node/WASM and through actual Chrome before timing.

| Direct-author commitment | Core mean / median / p95 ms | Imported nostr-tools mean / median / p95 ms |
|---|---:|---:|
| Schema 2, 970-byte event | 0.521 / 0.500 / 0.600 | 0.850 / 0.800 / 1.000 |
| Schema 3, 64 piece hashes, 5,422-byte event | 0.649 / 0.600 / 0.700 | 1.038 / 1.000 / 1.200 |

These measure the complete `verifySegmentCommitment` browser call, including
JSON marshalling, validation, signature checks and returned-content decoding.
The schema-3 event commits to a 4 MiB segment; the segment payload is not hashed
or transferred in this timing. Each profile/variant has 50 warm-up calls and
600 timed calls in six alternating-order rounds of 100. The vector timestamp
is fixed for replay. Timings exclude network transfer, module compilation and
player startup; Chrome's timer resolution limits individual-call precision.

## Experiment boundary

The baseline keeps BIP-340 checks inside `event::verify_event`. In the isolated
prototype, the WASM implementation of that function serialises the event to a
host import. The host parses it and calls `nostr-tools/pure.verifyEvent`,
returning the verdict; native Rust keeps its existing implementation. The
prototype browser adapter supplies that import. Both demo clients are built
with identical esbuild settings. Temporary source edits are restored after
the experiment, and neither experimental module nor adapter is shipped.

Every callback parses a fresh event object, so `nostr-tools` cannot reuse an
object's cached verification symbol. The timing includes this JSON callback
cost and all checks the current core invokes. A different import format,
authorisation cache or direct JavaScript verifier could change the result;
those alternatives were not measured. Timing covers two direct-author
profiles, while the conformance check covers all 140 shared vectors.

This is one desktop loopback measurement. It does not measure mobile battery,
physical iPhone/Android devices, public NAT, player-level latency or field load.
It changes no release, tag, package dependency or production verification path.

---

Source: [docs/NATIVE-REALTIME.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/NATIVE-REALTIME.md)

# Native operator real-time backend

Experimental, initiator-only transport for opaque datagrams. It does not
capture, encode, decrypt, record or play media. The existing browser adapter,
NIP-44 session, application admission and media queues remain separate.

`src/node/native-realtime.mjs` loads no native dependency on import. A dedicated
operator supplies a source-built **node-datachannel 0.33.4** addon whose
native library identifies itself as **0.24.5-forgesworn-turn-close.1**. Both
versions are checked. The stock npm binary is refused. Browser consumers
load no native code; explicit preparation belongs to the operator build.

## API and ownership

```js
import { createRequire } from 'node:module';
import { readPreparedNativeRealtime } from './scripts/build-native-realtime.mjs';
const directory = '/absolute/path/to/prepared-native';
const { receipt } = await readPreparedNativeRealtime(directory);
const binding = directory + '/native-addon.node';
const nodeDataChannel = createRequire(binding)(binding);
import { createNativeRealtimeBackend } from './src/node/native-realtime.mjs';

const backend = await createNativeRealtimeBackend({
  nodeDataChannel,
  packageVersion: receipt.bindingVersion,
  maxPacketLifeTimeMs: 250,
  maxPeers: 16,
});

// Pass backend.RTCPeerConnectionImpl to RealtimePeer on the operator side,
// with initiator:true and the same explicit finite lifetime. The browser
// installs its answerer before the operator starts sending an offer.
// ICE servers and all/relay policy remain explicit application inputs.

backend.closeOwnedPeers();
// Only at dedicated process exit, after every call has closed:
backend.disposeForProcessExit();
```

The factory returns `RTCPeerConnectionImpl`, `closeOwnedPeers`, `snapshot` and
`disposeForProcessExit`. `closeOwnedPeers` closes all peers it created and
refuses new ones. It does not call the dependency's process-global cleanup.
`disposeForProcessExit` also invokes that global cleanup exactly once; it is
unsuitable as the cleanup operation for one call in a shared native process.

The facade implements the subset used by `RealtimePeer`: offer creation,
local offer application, remote answer application, trickled ICE, state and
data-channel events, bounded binary sends, buffering observations and close.
It is not a complete browser RTCPeerConnection polyfill. Native automatic
channel negotiation has already applied an offer when `createOffer` resolves.

## Initiator boundary

The upstream 0.33.4 polyfill caches channel reliability attributes from
constructor options. For an incoming channel it supplies no options, so
those attributes describe defaults rather than the actual remote DCEP mode.
The native binding exposes no reliability getter. This adapter therefore
**refuses remote offers, answer creation and all incoming channels**.

It creates one exact `relayswarm-live-v1` channel locally, requesting unordered
delivery and the configured finite lifetime. Its exposed attributes describe
that local native request. The actual browser answerer independently checks
the remote channel's negotiated DCEP values and refuses mismatches. The
operator must not select this backend as an answerer or relabel unknown
remote channels to pass the shared policy gate.

ICE starts with no default STUN server. The host must supply `iceServers`
and `iceTransportPolicy`; relay policy is not downgraded. TURN credentials
use the native structured ICE API, preserving opaque colons, slashes and plus
signs instead of interpolating them into URI user-info. DTLS fingerprint
verification remains enabled. Native logging is initialised at `None`; there
is no per-call log writer in this module. Host/provider logging is separate.

The pinned native libjuice backend supports **TURN over UDP only**. This
facade refuses TURN/TCP and TURN/TLS configuration before allocating a peer,
including under `all` policy, so unsupported servers cannot be silently
ignored in favour of a direct connection. This limit belongs to the native
backend; it is not a claim that the browser or Spry lacks those transports.

Native `send(false)` means the message was accepted into a buffer, not refused.
The shared datagram link checks native `bufferedAmount` before sending. This
facade preserves the standard void-send behaviour and treats native
exceptions as failure. Finite transport expiry and receiver observations
remain relevant; accepted-send counters alone do not prove delivery.

## Qualification

```sh
node --test test/native-realtime.test.mjs
node scripts/build-native-realtime.mjs --output target/realtime-native
E2E_NATIVE_ARTIFACT=/absolute/path/to/target/realtime-native \
  node test/native-realtime-browser.mjs
E2E_NATIVE_BINDING=/absolute/path/to/target/realtime-native/native-addon.node \
  python3 test/native-turn-lifecycle.py
```

The browser command verifies the explicit prepared receipt and binary, then
fails on missing, altered or mismatched inputs. There is no successful skipped mode. An optional
`E2E_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE` selects a host-installed test browser. It exercises
the real native initiator against a real Chromium answerer through encrypted
RelaySwarm signalling and verifies actual browser DCEP reliability, binary
datagrams containing NUL/255 in both directions and rejection of an unexpected
incoming channel. Its finite process closes peers, relay, browser and native
runtime. It captures no camera, microphone, screen or media recording.

Initial macOS arm64 loopback qualification passed on the development Mac
and M4 with Node 24, package 0.33.4 and native library 0.24.5. The M4 run used
an isolated temporary source copy and existing dependencies without changing
shared installations. [Retained observations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/evidence/native-realtime-loopback-20261024.json)
record the exact gate. This is not Linux runtime acceptance,
public-NAT performance, multi-participant media acceptance or a release.

### Stock TURN allocation-release finding

The stock 0.33.4/0.24.5 native backend failed a separate allocation-release
gate against an authenticated synthetic loopback TURN server. Both the raw
binding and this facade obtained a relay candidate, returned from close and
process-global cleanup, and released their local UDP socket while the process
was still alive. Neither sent `Refresh(lifetime=0)`. Socket ownership cleanup
therefore does not establish prompt release of a server allocation.
[Retained observations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/evidence/native-turn-close-stock-20261024.json) keep
that failure distinct from the passing browser/datagram gate.

`test/native-turn-release.py` reproduces the check with fixture credentials;
it contacts no live relay and exits unsuccessfully when release is missing.
It requires an explicit exact `E2E_NATIVE_PACKAGE_ROOT`; `PROBE_MODE=facade`
selects the owned wrapper and `E2E_NATIVE_BINDING` can explicitly select a
separately built sidecar. A native-source correction needs independent
identity, source/patch/binary receipts and release qualification. Reissuing
credentials, increasing quota or restarting a relay does not repair teardown.

## Dependency and licence boundary

This adapter's original source follows RelaySwarm's MIT licence. The native
dependency is separately **MPL-2.0**; the combined distribution must not be
labelled MIT-only. Binary packaging must retain its licence/notices and make
the covered source, including any modifications, available as required by
that licence. The prepared artifact includes the reviewed dependency licence inventory,
exact source revisions, complete patches and hashes of its emitted files.
Modified MPL-covered files are libjuice `src/agent.c`, `src/agent.h` and
libdatachannel `include/rtc/version.h`; SCTP source is unchanged.

Primary pinned sources:

- [node-datachannel 0.33.4 package](https://registry.npmjs.org/node-datachannel/0.33.4)
- [Native binding source and licence](https://github.com/murat-dogan/node-datachannel/tree/v0.33.4)
- [Pinned native build configuration](https://github.com/murat-dogan/node-datachannel/blob/v0.33.4/CMakeLists.txt)
- [libdatachannel 0.24.5 source and licence](https://github.com/paullouisageneau/libdatachannel/tree/v0.24.5)
- [Buffered-send contract](https://github.com/paullouisageneau/libdatachannel/blob/v0.24.5/include/rtc/channel.hpp)

### Source-built allocation teardown

Explicit preparation builds only pinned source inputs with at most two jobs.
Each invocation owns fresh source and derived directories; it never trusts an
existing OpenSSL/CMake cache or modifies an installed npm prebuild. The
receipt and library version identify a modified binary. Preparation downloads
sources; importing the verifier or starting an operator never does.

The libjuice change sends explicit authenticated `Refresh(lifetime=0)` on the
existing allocation socket before destroying it. Receive processing remains
alive for stale-nonce challenges; a single closing loop owns retries and
transaction IDs. Each agent has a 500ms deadline and at most six requests per
allocation. A 438 updates the nonce and starts a fresh transaction. Validated
success with explicit lifetime zero, or allocation-mismatch 437, completes
release. Success validation uses upstream transaction IDs and MESSAGE-INTEGRITY;
upstream error handling does not require error-response integrity. This patch
does not introduce a general TURN response-source validation change.

Release is best effort under packet loss or partition: an unreachable server
can retain its allocation until expiry. Eight serial fully blackholed agents
can consume approximately four seconds plus scheduling overhead. This bound
is per agent, not per process. No credential rotation or quota increase is a
substitute for cleanup.

`test/native-turn-lifecycle.py` uses only authenticated synthetic loopback TURN
with a cap of eight and one unchanged fixture credential. It checks normal
and dropped-request `8 → 0 → 8 → 0` reuse, delayed 350ms stale-nonce challenges,
invalid-HMAC and wrong-transaction success replies, lost/late acknowledgements,
and bounded whole-process cleanup when all release packets are blackholed.
[The retained macOS arm64 lifecycle run](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/evidence/native-turn-lifecycle-20261024.json)
passed all eight scenarios. Normal, dropped-first-two and delayed-nonce cases
each released and reused eight slots twice. All-eight blackhole cleanup
returned in 4254ms while the fake server correctly retained eight allocations.
[Patched native/browser qualification](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/evidence/native-realtime-patched-loopback-20261024.json)
also passed actual unordered 250ms DCEP and binary exchange. These are
synthetic loopback gates; Linux runtime and public Spry lifecycle acceptance
remain separate.

Every accepted release request must carry the correct HMAC, realm, username,
nonce and original client UDP tuple. Blackhole allocation retention is an
expected limitation, reported separately from successful release.

Neither native implementation, operator independence nor absent call logs
establishes an Online Safety Act exemption.

---

Source: [docs/NIP-DRAFT.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/NIP-DRAFT.md)

# RelaySwarm experimental protocol draft

This is a local specification of the implemented RelaySwarm session and browser
object contracts. It is **not an accepted Nostr NIP**. Session wire version 3,
commitment schemas 1 to 3, browser object framings 1 and 2 and native object
framing have separate version boundaries. Schema 3 and framing 2 are
experimental and off by default. The original `poc.mjs` uses older plaintext
signalling and must not be described as this encrypted contract.

## Session events

Every event uses NIP-01 canonical serialisation and a valid BIP-340 signature.
The swarm identifier is exactly one `x` tag. Signal events have exactly one `p`
recipient tag. Presence events must not contain recipient tags. Senders use
throwaway Nostr identities; presence does not establish a trusted media author.

| Contract | Implemented value |
|----------|-------------------|
| Presence kind | `24170` |
| Signal kind | `24171` |
| Session version | JSON field `v: 3` |
| Signal encryption | Pairwise NIP-44 v2; mandatory |
| Sender event age | At most 120 seconds old; at most 30 seconds ahead |
| Presence JSON limit | 16 KiB UTF-8 |
| Signal ciphertext limit | 64 KiB UTF-8 |
| Decrypted signal limit | 8 KiB UTF-8 |
| Relay frame limit | 1 MiB |

Presence content has this shape:

```json
{"v":3,"role":"watcher","transports":[{"type":"webrtc","publicKey":"<64 lowercase hex characters>"}],"have":[],"open":true}
```

`role` and transport `type` are lowercase tokens, up to 32 characters, matching
`[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*`. `transports` is required and contains at most eight entries.
A capability may carry `obj`, its browser object framing version, an integer
from 1 to 15; absent reads as 1, and other values reject the presence. v0.2.1
accepts the field and discards it.
`have` is required and contains at most 32 lowercase 64-character hexadecimal
object keys. `open` is optional and advisory. An optional opaque `ticket` is a
non-empty string of at most 2 KiB UTF-8; admission is the host's responsibility.
A browser WebRTC capability uses the peer's Nostr public key. A native
`hyperdht-v1` capability uses its DHT transport public key.

Signal plaintext has this shape, then the whole JSON object is NIP-44 encrypted:

```json
{"v":3,"type":"offer","transport":"webrtc","requestId":"<request identifier>","payload":{"sdp":"<complete SDP>"}}
```

`type` and `transport` use the same token rule. `requestId` is 8–64 ASCII
characters from `[a-zA-Z0-9_-]`. `payload` is an object. Browser offers, answers
and rejects must match the pending counterparty, transport and request ID.
SDP appears in `payload.sdp`. Browser admission is checked before revealing an
answer and again after asynchronous negotiation. Native `dial` and `ready`
payloads bind the transport public key, expected SHA-256 and exact object size;
see [Native transport](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/NATIVE-TRANSPORT.md).

A peer must not reinterpret a missing version or an unsupported version as
plaintext. RelaySwarm's current session rejects version 2. The NIP-44 encryption
version is not the RelaySwarm session version.

## Browser object exchange

A WebRTC data channel carries JSON text controls and binary chunks. At most one
response is in flight in each direction. A binary chunk is at most 16 KiB.

| Message | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| `{"t":"have","keys":["<key>"]}` | Complete advertised key set, capped at 256 |
| `{"t":"have","add":["<key>"],"del":[]}` | Bounded key-set update |
| `{"t":"want","id":1,"k":"<key>"}` | Request one object |
| `{"t":"meta","id":1,"size":262181}` | Exact response size; chunks follow |
| Binary messages | Response bytes, serialised between `meta` and `eof` |
| `{"t":"eof","id":1}` | Response complete |
| `{"t":"none","id":1}` | Object unavailable or serving declined |
| `{"t":"cancel","id":1}` | Receiver no longer wants the response |

Control text is capped at 64 KiB. Object size is limited by the host's configured
segment cap, at most 16 MiB. `meta` cannot override the independently verified
commitment size. Repeated headers, excessive chunks, empty chunks and response
size overflow close the link. Timeout or cancellation resolves the request
without extending its deadline. On a known ordered, fully reliable channel,
the receiver may discard the remaining response while keeping the link busy
until a matching, size-validated `eof`, or `none` before any metadata. No new
request can reuse untagged chunks during that interval. Such a receiver sends
`cancel` for the request. A holder that honours it answers with `none` before
`meta`, or stops sending chunks and sends `eof` early; only after sending
`cancel` does a receiver accept an `eof` with fewer bytes than `meta` announced.
A holder ignores `cancel` for a request it is not queuing or sending, and peers
that do not implement it ignore the message and send the response in full.
The existing bounded drain timeout closes an incomplete response; unknown or partially reliable
channels close immediately. Host stop and admission withdrawal still close
immediately. Upload queues and backpressure retain their original bounds.
Framing 2 adds a piece range `"p":[start,end]` to `want` and `meta`, with `end`
exclusive and `0 <= start < end <= 64`. Pieces are those of commitment schema 3,
whose piece size is a function of the object size alone, so both sides derive
the byte offsets without exchanging them. A holder that has the object answers
with `meta` echoing the same range and `size` equal to the range's exact byte
length, then those bytes; a range past the held object's last piece is answered
with `none`. A malformed range closes the link. The requester closes the link
when `meta` omits or changes the range or its size differs, which is how a
framing 1 holder that ignores `p` and sends the whole object is detected. A
requester sends `p` only to a holder whose current presence advertises
`obj: 2` or higher, and a viewer advertises framing 2 only while every one of
its links can serve ranges. A holder charges a ranged response against upload
allowances by the bytes it sends. Requests without `p` behave exactly as in
framing 1.

Optional `contribution` and `fetching` controls coordinate serving and short
fetch leases; they are advisory and never authorise media or spend upload
allowance.

An object key identifies the host's canonical media URL/range within a swarm;
it is **not** the content digest. The local publisher uses SHA-256 over
`swarmId + "\n" + path`, appending `#start-end` for an exclusive-end byte range.
Hosts with CDN aliases or query-bearing URLs must define their trust policy
explicitly. A peer's `have` claim or `meta` message never establishes provenance.

## Signed media commitments

Commitments use kind `24172`, one `x` swarm tag and one `e` tag naming the stable
stream authorisation event. That event is signed by the trusted media author,
has kind `30311`, one `d` identifier and explicit
`["relayswarm","redistribute","1"]` consent.

Schema 1 uses domain `relayswarm-segment-v1` and binds the stream event ID, swarm,
object key, numeric rendition, sequence, discontinuity, part index or `null`,
SHA-256, exact size and expiry. Schema 2 uses `relayswarm-segment-v2` and adds
`playlist`, `mediaType` and `encryption`; its `rendition` is the exact playlist
identity. This avoids treating player level indices, which codec filtering can
renumber, as trusted media identities. Content must equal the canonical field
order emitted by `commitmentContent` in
[segment-commitment.mjs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/src/browser/segment-commitment.mjs).

Schema 3 uses `relayswarm-segment-v3` and adds `pieceSize` and `pieces` to the
schema 2 fields, after `encryption`. `pieceSize` must equal
`ceil(max(65536, ceil(size / 64)) / 16384) * 16384`: at least 64 KiB, at most 64
pieces, a multiple of 16 KiB. `pieces` holds exactly `ceil(size / pieceSize)`
lowercase SHA-256 digests, one per piece in order; the last piece may be
short. A receiver may verify and keep each piece as it arrives, from any
source, and still requires the whole object to match `sha256` and `size`
before delivery to the player. The local publisher signs schema 3 instead of
schema 2, never both, when its `pieceCommitments` option is set. v0.2.1 and
RelaySwarmKit v0.5.0 reject schema 3, so their viewers load those segments
from origin.

The receiver independently matches every context field. Commitments are at
most 120 seconds old, at most 30 seconds ahead and expire within 300 seconds of
verification. The local publisher normally signs for 60 seconds. Size is
positive and within the host's segment cap. The actual received bytes must
match the signed size and SHA-256 before delivery to the player.

Schema 2 permits alternate audio and complete LL-HLS parts. Delta playlists
require a bounded previously verified catalogue; a cold delta cannot establish
omitted contexts. Init maps remain HTTP assets. Identity AES-128 requires an
explicit publication policy and signs ciphertext plus exact key URI/IV
metadata. Content keys stay on the HTTP path and are never peer objects.
SAMPLE-AES, DRM, subtitle and I-frame rendition publication are unsupported.

## Scoped commitment delegation

Kind `24173`, domain `relayswarm-commitment-delegation-v1`, authorises one
commitment public key under the trusted author's signature. Its canonical
content binds `streamEventId`, `swarmId`, `delegatePubkey`, `notBefore`,
`expiresAt`, `renditions`, `mediaTypes`, `allowParts` and `maxSegmentBytes`.
Scopes contain at most 40 exact rendition identifiers. Delegation expires no
later than one hour after issuance. A delegated commitment includes
`["delegation","<delegation event ID>"]`, matches every scope restriction and
cannot outlive the delegation.

Kind `24174`, domain `relayswarm-commitment-revocation-v1`, revokes an exact
delegation ID under the same author's signature, stream and swarm. Hosts supply
a bounded current revocation view or explicit revoked IDs. Verifiers do not
query relays and absence from a supplied view does not prove global absence of
revocation. Replacing the trusted stream authorisation also invalidates scopes
bound to its old event ID. A delegate is not authorised to sign live metadata.

## Live metadata and stable authorisation

The local publisher keeps the minimal commitment authorisation stable across
restarts. A separate full NIP-53 kind `30311` advertisement uses address
`live-<stable authorisation event ID>`, so renewing live status does not replace
the event to which commitments and delegations bind. Its signed tags include
`streaming`, `status`, `starts`, `expiration`, `relays`,
`relayswarm-authorisation` and `relayswarm-swarm`. Ended advertisements include
`ends`. The RelaySwarm-specific linking tags are experimental extensions.

Advertisements expire within five minutes and require HTTPS/WSS endpoints.
Loopback HTTP/WS requires explicit test opt-in. Discovery pins the linked
stable authorisation using `streamAuthorisations`, checks the same author and
host-selected swarm, and preserves the host's allowed origins, relay and ICE
policies. Event-suggested endpoints cannot expand those policies. The latest
ended, withdrawn or unsafe update suppresses older live metadata. The host
must obtain current metadata; a stable signature alone does not prove that a
stream is still live. `previousEvent` gives immediate lifecycle updates a later
creation timestamp within the allowed clock tolerance, avoiding an addressable
event ID tie. Standard NIP-53 fields are described in the
[upstream draft](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/53.md).

## Historical Swift baseline and current interoperability

On 13 October 2026, `test/interop-swift.mjs` tested public RelaySwarmKit revision
[`7eb042ee0fc0e960780c61d755a2ec50f1a8be40`](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm-kit/tree/7eb042ee0fc0e960780c61d755a2ec50f1a8be40)
with its pinned secp256k1 dependency and macOS arm64 libdatachannel binary.

| Gate | Measured result |
|------|-----------------|
| Unmodified Kit `SwarmSignaller` ↔ RelaySwarm v3 | Incompatible in both directions |
| Kit NIP-44/signatures ↔ JavaScript | Compatible in the exercised encrypted session |
| Explicit Swift v3 fixture adapter ↔ JavaScript session | Encrypted presence/offer/answer journey passed |
| Kit libdatachannel ↔ JavaScript werift/production `PeerLink` | 262,181-byte transfer in 17 chunks passed |
| Independent Swift commitment verification | 12 schema/context/signature/expiry cases passed |
| Corrupted bytes over the real WebRTC channel | Rejected against the signed commitment |
| Plaintext and malformed encrypted session probes | Rejected by the fixture adapter |
| Published Swift v3 client, physical devices, NAT variety | Not proved at that baseline checkpoint |
| Kit ↔ HyperDHT native transport | Unsupported by the inspected Kit |

The test adapter uses unchanged pinned toolkit crypto, relay and WebRTC
components, but adds a separate strict v3 envelope parser and browser object
receiver inside this repository. Its passing journey **does not establish
compatibility of the Kit client at that revision**. That baseline Kit uses
presence version 2, signal version tags and top-level `type`/`sdp`, and retains a
plaintext fallback. Current RelaySwarm accepts none of those as v3 sessions.

Run `node test/interop-swift.mjs --evidence artifacts/relayswarm-swift-interop-current.json`
on macOS arm64 with Swift and authenticated read-only `gh` access. It fetches
exact public component sources into an owned scratch package, compiles with four
jobs, records source hashes and results, then removes its downloads/build and
fixture services after success. The named receipt is retained. A failed build
keeps owned scratch for diagnosis and reuse; remove it once its evidence is
recorded. No external repository is edited.

### Historical Kit migration requirements

These requirements guided the subsequent RelaySwarmKit upgrade:

1. Update `Sources/RelaySwarmSignalling/Swarm.swift` to emit/require `v:3`,
   transport, request ID and nested payloads; require NIP-44 for every signal.
   Remove automatic plaintext fallback from the default API. If legacy support
   remains, expose it through a separately named opt-in API and never negotiate
   down from v3.
2. Extend presence with bounded transport capabilities, object keys, optional
   upload availability and opaque host admission tickets. Apply the v3 age,
   recipient uniqueness, payload and byte limits before dispatch.
3. Update `Sources/RelaySwarmTransport/SwarmHost.swift` so answers preserve the
   pending request ID and transport, with admission before disclosing SDP.
   Supply bounded `have`/`want`/`meta`/binary/`eof` framing rather than assuming
   arbitrary host broadcasts are authenticated HLS objects.
4. Add an independent signed commitment module covering schemas 1 and 2,
   current author/delegation/revocation trust, exact fragment context and byte
   verification. Preserve receive-only/upload-consent semantics in the consuming
   application; a verified commitment is not viewer consent to serve.
5. Run this real interop journey against the updated public APIs, without the
   fixture adapter, and add Swift negative tests for version downgrade,
   misrouted/replayed events, context confusion, chunk floods and cancellation.
   Release and pin that tested Kit revision before publishing compatibility
   claims. HyperDHT support would be a separate transport implementation.


The concrete [Kit review proposal](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/interop/README.md) includes an exact-source
patch and SHA-256 manifest. Its full local SDK suite passed 25 tests with one
public-relay test skipped. The later authorised upgrade adds public signed-media
APIs and is published as [Kit v0.5.0](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm-kit/releases/tag/v0.5.0)
at `2f0b26ace4096a5dca87baf715274f91c331ac3a`. PR and merged-head CI passed
39 tests with one opt-in public-relay skip. The production browser sender and
current `SwarmGuest`, `MediaDataChannel` and `SignedMediaTransfer` APIs completed
author/delegate transfers of 108,950 fMP4 HLS bytes; corruption, tampering and
pre-request/during-transfer revocation each returned zero bytes. No wire adapter
was used. The exact source/receipt boundary and remaining physical/NAT/playback
responsibilities are in the [interop guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/interop/README.md).
