# Pilot operator controls

[Documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/README.md) · [Broadcaster](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/BROADCASTING.md) · [Container deployment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/deploy/README.md) · [API](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/API.md) · [Evidence](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md)

These controls belong to **v0.2.1** and are absent from v0.1.0 assets. It adds bounded admission, durable reporting and crash supervision; final production acceptance remains open. See [production features](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/PRODUCTION-FEATURES.md) and [Status](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md).

Before the first broadcast is ready, the root returns an HTTP 200 waiting page with a three-second refresh. Other endpoints return HTTP 503 with `Retry-After: 3`, including the authenticated status route; the waiting listener exposes no session, relay or operator API. The launcher replaces it with the player on the same port when both renditions publish. Waiting-page reachability does not establish fresh media, successful decoding or a verified public deployment.

## Credentials and HTTP routes

The broadcaster creates its private `operator-token` in `--state-dir`. The demo can instead take `--operator-token-file FILE`, the `RELAYSWARM_OPERATOR_TOKEN` environment variable, or the `startDemoServer` JavaScript option `operatorToken`. Prefer a private file; supplying both JavaScript token sources is rejected. Tokens must contain 32–256 non-whitespace characters. Token files require an owner-controlled canonical parent, a 0600 regular single-link file and matching ownership; symlinks and unsafe permissions are rejected.

The token is never in the player page, `/session.json`, public policy or operator status. Keep it separate from publisher signing secrets and forwarding credentials. The [deployment guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/deploy/README.md#operator-access-and-private-identity) shows private header-file extraction and curl commands without printing the token or placing it in arguments.

| Route | Method/authentication | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `/operator/status` | GET, `Authorization: Bearer TOKEN` | Policy, origin HTTP counters, publisher work/cache metrics, report aggregate, bounded request diagnostics and optional redacted broadcast worker/publication status |
| `/operator/policy` | POST, bearer token, `application/json` | Accepts only `{"mode":null}`, `{"mode":"off"}`, `{"mode":"shadow"}` or `{"mode":"peer-first"}`; returns incremented policy revision |
| `/delivery-policy.json` | GET, public | Mode, revision and reporting availability; no token or publisher secret |
| `/delivery-policy.json?session=1` | GET, public, advertised by the current source | Policy plus the same public session snapshot as `/session.json`; no extra authentication or credentials |
| `/reports` | POST, explicit server enablement and same-origin browser request | Accepts only bounded numeric measurement fields |
| `/operator/admission` | POST, bearer token | Revokes a key or rotates the ticket epoch |
| `/admission/challenge`, `/admission/ticket`, `/admission/verify` | POST, same-origin | Bounded key-possession challenge, short-lived ticket and live verification |

Unconfigured operator controls return 503; absent/incorrect credentials return 401. Cross-site Origin/Fetch-Metadata requests are rejected. Operator bodies are capped at 2,048 bytes and reject unknown fields/invalid modes; wrong methods and content types are rejected. Authentication is not a replacement for HTTPS, host protection or restricting administrative exposure at the reverse proxy. The bearer token grants policy/status access, not media-source credentials or shell access.

## Policy and viewer consent

`mode: null` leaves mode choice to the viewer. `off` requests origin-only playback. `shadow` or `peer-first` selects behaviour **only after the viewer has chosen a peer mode**: viewer origin-only selection and `Use origin only` always win. A policy can never opt the viewer into uploading. Valid publisher-signed redistribution authorisation is also required by the browser engine; operator policy is not an authorisation bypass.

The page checks policy and publisher session every two seconds, with at most
three independent checks pending. Authority expires five seconds after a
check was issued; response arrival cannot extend it. v0.2.1
advertises `deliveryPolicySession: "inline-v1"` and returns both public snapshots
in one response from `/delivery-policy.json?session=1`. Older server descriptors
retain the two parallel requests. Missing or malformed advertised session data
fails closed; it does not trigger a legacy fallback. Bare policy and operator
responses keep their existing shapes. Programmatic hosts can use
`startDemoServer({policySessionSnapshot: false})` for the legacy contract.

Disablement is cooperative browser behaviour, not immediate revocation of
already delivered media. An observed operator OFF takes effect before session
validation or admission work. Expired authority restores origin loading and
clears upload/reporting consent; later success cannot restore those opt-ins.
Playback's video instance remains running; origin availability still determines
whether playback continues. Same-manifest identity changes rejoin without
resetting page counters. A changed manifest fails to origin rather than guessing.
The combined response reduces request count; it has no new deployed field
qualification and does not guarantee uninterrupted authority.

## Upload and measurement limits

The page offers 10 MB, 100 MB (default) or 1 GB of cumulative **media payload** allowance, plus a separate upload rate choice. Web Locks and origin storage reserve payloads atomically across settings, rejoining, reloads and tabs. Interrupted sends are not refunded; oversized next segments do not spend the smaller balance. Exhaustion stops contribution while playback continues. Storage failure disables uploading. Consent is requested anew after reload; the viewer can explicitly raise or reset the allowance. This local allowance covers one browser profile at the origin.

The current source also offers an optional [shared account allowance](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/ACCOUNT-UPLOAD-BUDGET.md), using explicit Nostr sign-in or the integrating website's authenticated account. Devices using one identity and ledger share cumulative reservations in addition to their local allowances. Account connection, linking, settings changes and resets leave uploading off until fresh viewer consent. Keep the private ledger through upgrades; disconnecting or reloading does not refund its charges. Neither allowance counts complete physical wire traffic. The deployed `44b21d6` pilot offers Nostr sign-in; no website resolver is configured there.

The library option is `maxUploadBytesPerSession`; omission means unlimited and zero means no media uploads. Its metrics expose configured cap, remaining allowance and exhaustion. Host applications that recreate a swarm must carry their own cumulative allowance forward, as the page does. Rate limits use a token bucket with up to a two-second burst. Signalling, transport overhead, commitment fetches and shadow downloads are additional traffic; an upload media cap is not a wire-traffic limit.

Server `origin` counters separate `/media/` requests/body bytes from commitment requests/body bytes. Media counts include playlists, init segments, ranges and error responses; HEAD contributes no response body. Body bytes are bytes handed to HTTP responses, not confirmed physical-wire totals or network overhead. Browser resource timings have their own scope and exclude native-HLS requests. Verified peer payload records media accepted from peers; shadow mode adds peer traffic alongside origin loading. None of these counters alone establish net traffic/cost savings.

Publisher metrics include signing/hashing/cache activity, concurrent work and rejections. Broadcast metrics include worker states/restarts, rendition shape, generation and last publication time; they contain no input/output URLs or stream keys. A running process does not prove a fresh source, successful decoding or platform acceptance.

## Diagnosing control-path timeouts

v0.2.1 adds a numeric `Server-Timing: rs-app;dur=...` header to
session, policy, admission, report and commitment responses. It measures handler
entry to response headers. It excludes queueing before the handler, network
transport and response-body receipt. Media responses are not instrumented.

Authenticated status includes `requestDiagnostics`: seven fixed route labels,
128 active observations, a 30-second observation expiry and the latest 120
one-second windows. Histograms distinguish headers from terminal outcomes
(finished, cancelled or expired). A server finish means handing the response to
the HTTP stack, rather than confirmation that the browser received it. Event-loop
delay, scheduler drift and utilisation accompany each completed window. The
sampler is unreferenced and closes with the server. No request identities, IPs,
URLs, query strings, headers, bodies or credentials are stored in these aggregates.

Downloaded page receipts include `controlTimings`, with at most 64 numeric
observations and 64 pending observations, measuring headers and JSON-body time
separately. Application-header duration is included when available. Caller
signals, timeouts and single-request behaviour remain unchanged. These local
timings are not submitted as numeric reports and do not grant upload or reporting
consent. Durations above one minute are clipped and counted.

For matched probes, run the following **on the server hosting the loopback
endpoint**, using its configured public origin:

```sh
node scripts/probe-control-path.mjs \
  --public-origin https://trial.example \
  --loopback-origin http://127.0.0.1:8787 \
  --duration 60000 --interval 5000 --timeout 5000
```

The probe is bounded to five minutes, verifies public TLS, retains numeric
observations only and discards response bodies after a byte limit. Its fresh
HTTP/1.1 connections differ from browser HTTP/2. Pair these observations with
actual failure timestamps; the instrumentation cannot retroactively diagnose
an earlier incident or establish a network cause from a healthy later sample.

## Optional numeric reporting

Reporting is **off by default**. Enable it server-side using `--telemetry` or `startDemoServer({telemetry:true})`; each viewer must then check the separate reporting opt-in. The page sends cumulative numeric snapshots every fifteen seconds after playback starts. Downloadable field receipts remain separate and are not submitted.

Reports use `{v:1, reportId, sequence, values}`. The temporary page ID is 32 hex characters; sequence increases for new cumulative snapshots. Values contain exactly `durationMs`, `peerBytes`, `uploadedBytes`, `originMediaRequests`, `originMediaBytes`, `stalls`, `stallMs` and `fatalErrors`, non-negative safe integers up to 10¹². No account, browser version, device/network labels or peer IP addresses are accepted. Infrastructure still sees connection addresses; there is no third-party report endpoint.

The collector permits 240 requests per ten seconds, caps bodies at 2,048 bytes and requires same-origin requests. Retention defaults to 256 page IDs for five minutes; `reportCapacity` and `reportTtlMs` bound it. With `operatorState` (CLI `--operator-state`) enabled, private state survives restart and expiry is applied after reopening. Retries are idempotent, stale sequences do not add traffic again, and decreased counters are refused. The pending durable write queue defaults to 64; overload returns 503. Reports remain untrusted observations, not unique-viewer totals or billing evidence. Broadcasters enable private operational persistence automatically.

## Resources and admission boundary

The HTTP example caps active media responses at 32, connections at 128, header size at 8 KiB and request/header timeouts at ten seconds. Commitment requests have a separate 240-per-ten-second budget. Publisher defaults permit eight concurrent commitment operations and 512 entries in each hash/commitment cache; playlist/catalogue/segment bounds are documented in the [API](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/API.md). Cancellation releases media file handles and response slots even while lookup/opening is pending.

The [container package](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/deploy/README.md) sets CPU, memory, process and log limits, loopback ingest/player mappings and private network boundaries. Its healthcheck requires a recent publication and publishing worker state; it becomes unhealthy without input or during a prolonged source outage. Compose restart policies recover container exits, not unhealthy status alone. Measure actual host capacity before broadening a pilot.

The candidate demo supplies a bounded ticket issuer and live revocation checks. The embedded relay rejects unadmitted presence/signals and caps aggregate messages. Open issuance establishes bounded keys, not unique people or paid subscriptions; broader Sybil and real-network acceptance remain separate gates.

## Restart and recovery

Preserve the dedicated state directory/volume to retain publisher identity and operator credentials. Shut down normally so workers, file handles and the exclusive `.broadcast-lock` are released. Do not run two pipelines against one media directory, mount the state into unrelated services, or delete private state during an upgrade.

On supported local POSIX storage, permanent publication/worker lease inodes and a guardian permit automatic parent-crash recovery after all worker groups are reaped. A dirty guardian marker or legacy pre-lease lock requires explicit operator inspection. Never delete lease database files to force acquisition. A namespace-local PID is insufficient evidence; retain private backups and leave uncertain ownership closed. The [deployment guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/deploy/README.md#exclusive-volume-ownership-and-crash-recovery) describes the recovery boundary.

macOS durable state requires a writable APFS or HFS block filesystem with ownership enabled. RelaySwarm checks the exact directory and device identities through the system `df`, `diskutil` and `plutil` tools under one five-second deadline. Unsupported or changing identities, unavailable metadata and unconfirmed tool exit refuse acquisition.

Publisher state contains the signing secret; a whole-volume backup can also contain generated media. Use access-controlled encrypted backups. Forwarding credentials live in a separate private file and are read at launch; trusted process administrators can inspect ffmpeg's full URL arguments. Never put these secrets in a browser receipt, repository, public status response or issue attachment.

---

Source: [docs/PERFORMANCE.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/PERFORMANCE.md)

# Hot-path performance review

[Documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/README.md) · [Status](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md) · [Changelog](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/CHANGELOG.md)

Measured 24 October 2026, comparing the v0.4.3 source
`6f63fb2f8ae20a51953c80853816311f25980bf0` with the changes listed below. The
loader and publisher rows were measured against the earlier
`ed845ceccca192320f5b40b004ad54b7ffb2417c`; v0.4.3 changes neither the
loader's copy and hash paths nor the publisher. The host was a 4-vCPU x86-64 Linux VM with
Node 22.22.0 and Rust 1.94.1. Every figure is an in-memory micro-benchmark:
no browser, network, relay, device or player is involved, and timer resolution
and shared-host noise move single runs by 10–30%. Ranges are medians from
repeated runs. Compare runs on one host before and after a change; do not
compare absolute numbers across machines.

`npm run bench:hot-paths` reproduces the link, verification, multi-holder and
native-receive rows. It does not measure playback, field networks or battery.

## Changes and measurements

### Peer links and the WebAssembly boundary

| Path | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Core-backed link moving one 4 MiB object, both ends on one thread | 6.6–9.7 ms | 4.7–5.4 ms |
| Core module memory after two (or four) 4 MiB receives | 29.6 MiB | 17.3 MiB |
| Serving one 4 MiB schema-3 object as 16 piece ranges | 6.6–7.2 ms, 2.5 MiB module memory | 5.2–5.9 ms, 2.2 MiB |
| Multi-holder piece hashing in the core | 8.4–8.7 ms/MiB | 3.7 ms/MiB |
| Final whole-object check of a 4 MiB multi-holder transfer | 35–38 ms | 15–16 ms |

The JavaScript reference link moved the same object in 2.0–2.7 ms before and
after; it was not changed. v0.4.3 already passes only a requested range into
the module when serving; the range row shows the remaining frame copies.

- A link frame is moved, not copied, into the module's result buffer, and a
  resolved object is written into it once. The browser shell reads each event
  out of module memory separately, so a resolved object is copied once into a
  buffer of its exact size instead of copying the frame and then the object.
  The frame format is unchanged, so either module works with either shell.
- A receive whose size the caller expected from a signed commitment reserves
  that size once, on the first byte. A size only the remote declared still
  grows as bytes arrive, so `meta` alone holds no memory.
- The `sha2` crate is compiled at `opt-level = 3` while the rest of the module
  stays at `"z"`. The module grew from 411,690 to 415,896 bytes (152.0 to
  153.4 KB gzip), including the verdict memory below.
- The multi-holder transfer output is copied once, from module memory into its
  own buffer.

### Commitment verification

| Fresh commitment per segment, same stream event | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| JavaScript verifier, author-signed | 3.6–6.1 ms | 1.8–2.0 ms |
| WebAssembly verifier, author-signed | 0.80 ms | 0.51 ms |
| JavaScript verifier, delegate-signed with four revocations | 14.3–15.0 ms | 2.0–2.3 ms |
| WebAssembly verifier, delegate-signed with four revocations | 2.7–2.9 ms | 0.63–0.67 ms |

Both verifiers recheck the unchanged stream event, delegation and every
supplied revocation for every segment. Each now remembers up to 512 Schnorr
signatures it has proved, keyed by the recomputed event hash, public key and
signature. The hash is recomputed on every call, so a changed field is a
different key, and every other check (size bound, kind, tags, times, scope and
revocation matching) still runs on every call. Only proofs are remembered; a
failed signature is checked again. Both verifiers pass all 140 shared vectors
cold and again with every accepted signature remembered.

### Signalling and the native path

- `RelaySwarmSession` derives each peer's NIP-44 conversation key once, in a
  256-entry least-recently-used map cleared by `close()`. Fifty signals to one
  peer took 333 ms before and 162 ms after; the remainder is event signing.
  Signals stay pairwise encrypted.
- `RelayPool` gains `readyOnFirstRelay`. The installed native client uses it,
  so a relay that accepts TCP but never answers no longer holds discovery for
  the whole peer deadline. With one such relay and one healthy relay, a native
  fetch with a 4 s peer deadline completed over HyperDHT in about 0.2 s;
  before, it exhausted the deadline and the peer attempt failed.
- The native client starts Nostr discovery while the DHT bootstraps, and waits
  for both before dialling.
- The native receiver fills one buffer of the trusted size and hashes as bytes
  arrive, instead of keeping every chunk and joining them. A 16 MiB object in
  1,452-byte reads took 88–94 ms before and 23–24 ms after; in whole frames
  it took 22–24 ms before and 19 ms after, and peak memory is one object, not two.
  The size, chunk budget and digest checks are unchanged.

### Browser loader

Synchronous `load()` time per segment, with every counter identical before
and after:

| Case | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Shadow mode, unsampled, not serving, 2 MiB / 8 MiB | 1.92 / 3.90 ms | 0.12 / 0.14 ms |
| Peer-first HTTP fallback, not serving, 2 MiB / 8 MiB | 0.68 / 1.90 ms | 0.23 / 0.19 ms |

- Shadow mode copies origin bytes only for a sampled comparison or when
  serving is enabled (`serve: true`), and hashes them only for a sampled
  comparison. With the default 0.25 sample rate and serving off, three in four
  segments previously paid a copy and a SHA-256 they never used.
- Peer-first skips whole-segment copies when serving is not enabled or the
  object is already held. With serving enabled, bytes are still copied and the
  held-segment store decides when it runs, so a load that starts on cellular
  or without allowance and finishes with serving allowed is still held.
- The core-backed neighbour discovery keeps its decoded candidate list until
  a hint or clear changes it. With 64 candidates, `hinted` fell from 123–428 µs
  to 45–52 µs and `choose` from 150–399 µs to 70–78 µs.
- Trace-only clones are skipped when request tracing is off.

### Publisher and demo origin

| Path | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Catalogue refresh, live, two renditions of 12 segments | 1.1–1.3 ms | 0.8–0.9 ms |
| Catalogue refresh, two renditions of 1,800 segments | 12.8–13.7 ms | 0.9–1.0 ms |
| Commitment, 1,800-segment renditions with cache churn | 31–32 ms | 5.5–6.1 ms |
| 16 / 32 / 64 simultaneous requests for one new segment, limit 8 | 8 / 24 / 56 refused (503) | none refused, one signature |
| Account-allowance reservation at capacity (CPU) | 65 ms | 40 ms |
| Demo page assets, first visit / revalidation | 1.27 MB / 1.27 MB | 385 KB / 0 bytes (304) |
| Demo relay fan-out, 64 clients with two subscriptions | 430 µs per event | 53 µs per event |

- Media playlists are read concurrently, each read sized from its stat size,
  and a refresh whose master and media playlists are byte-identical to the
  previous read returns the previous parse. Every refresh still reads and
  stat-checks every playlist; a playlist with `EXT-X-SKIP` is always parsed,
  because a delta depends on the previous catalogue.
- Identical concurrent commitment requests join the one in flight without
  taking a slot. Each joined caller is then checked against a catalogue read
  and a file stat made after it arrived, as a separate request would be, so a
  context that left the playlist or a replaced segment is refused rather than
  answered from the earlier check. Each caller receives its own copy, and a
  failure reaches every joined caller and is not kept. The demo's
  240-per-10-second request budget is unchanged and still counts joined and
  cached requests.
- Account-allowance validation builds its account and grant indexes once,
  making it linear in the bounded state.
- The demo serves its page, style sheet, client bundle and WebAssembly module
  with Brotli or gzip, a strong ETag per encoding, `cache-control: no-cache`
  and 304 revalidation. Every other route keeps `no-store`, and the security
  headers are sent on 200 and 304 responses.
- The demo relay serialises each event once per fan-out, with byte-identical
  frames, and evicts history without copying it.

## Not changed

These were measured or reviewed and left alone, with the reason.

- Per-chunk link overhead is 5–9 µs in the core-backed link and 2–4 µs in the
  JavaScript link, about 1–2 ms per 4 MiB at both ends.
- Peer selection takes about 2 µs per choice with six links, and scheduler
  ticks about 13 µs.
- Incoming relay events are deduplicated before signature verification, and
  every bounded map in the session and relay pool stays bounded.

## Later changes (25 October 2026)

Measured on the same host against `5ed12be` (main after the changes above),
with in-memory or local-filesystem harnesses rather than a real encoder or
browser.

| Path | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Encoder playlist rename to republished playlist, both renditions | mean 135 ms, max 216 ms | mean 6 ms, max 28 ms |
| Allowance reservations, 8 at once | 571/s, slowest tenth 16 ms | 2,770/s, 5 ms |
| Allowance reservations, 32 at once | 436/s, slowest tenth 65 ms | 1,985/s, 20 ms |
| Allowance reservations, 64 at once | 399/s, slowest tenth 149 ms | 1,426/s, 56 ms |

- The broadcast publisher watches the current generation's rendition
  directories and publishes when the encoder renames `index.m3u8` into place.
  A new generation wakes it so the watch is in place before the first
  playlist. Events only wake the loop, which rereads and validates the files
  as before; segment events are ignored, events without a filename wake it at
  most every 10 ms, and the 250 ms interval remains the fallback. Blocking
  playlist reloads already watch the published playlists, so they release
  correspondingly sooner. The figures include the harness's own writes.
  `close()` during a publication no longer waits for another interval.
- The allowance ledger still applies operations one at a time in arrival
  order, each on its own copy of the state and checked for cancellation
  before and after it applies. Operations that queue while a write is in
  flight now share the next durable write and its two fsyncs. Once one of
  them has changed the state, every later outcome in the batch, refusals and
  reads included, is held until the write completes and released in arrival
  order; if that write fails, every operation in it is refused and none is
  kept. This host's fsync is fast, so slower storage gains more. A single
  reservation is unchanged.

## Follow-ups

Ranked by expected effect. None is implemented here.

1. Count only signatures, not joined or cached requests, against the demo's
   commitment budget, which otherwise caps a server near 48 viewers.
2. Keep a per-relay retry count so a relay that accepts and then drops each
   connection backs off instead of being redialled every 1–2 s.
3. Reduce per-reservation CPU at large ledger states: each operation still
   clones and validates the whole state.

Source: [docs/PRODUCTION-FEATURES.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/PRODUCTION-FEATURES.md)

# Production feature work

[Documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/README.md) · [Delivery requirements](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/PRODUCTION-READINESS.md) ·
[Evidence](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md) · [Protocol draft](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/NIP-DRAFT.md)

These changes belong to v0.2.1, the published experimental prerelease. They are
absent from the earlier v0.1.0 assets. Production acceptance remains a separate
gate; consult the delivery checklist for its current state.

## Browser delivery and media

Connected viewers exchange bounded contributor/rendition interests and short
origin-fetch leases. A contributor fetches fresh live media from HTTP while
other interested viewers may wait for verified peer availability within their
playback deadline. Peer claims are advisory: lack of availability, expiry,
invalid signatures or insufficient playback buffer use the HTTP loader.
Measured HTTP latency raises the origin reserve; peer transfer estimates
cannot spend the time retained for fallback. hls.js retains bitrate selection.

Commitment, admission and persistent-reservation host callbacks receive an
operation-specific signal. A deadline aborts that signal and stops waiting
for the result. Host callbacks must honour the signal to cancel their I/O.
The bundled demo passes it to its HTTP requests; stopped or expired operations
fence late results.

The demo retains fatal/native decoder records and allows one deferred attempt
to recover a fatal append/MediaSource-reset error. It restores the HTTP loader,
stops contribution, clears upload consent and retries the current live/VOD
position. Advancing playback must be observed within ten seconds; repeated
failure, user cancellation or publisher changes stop recovery. Budget state
is preserved. A recovered outcome does not erase the fatal error or establish
the cause of an earlier unrelated failure.

The same single repair budget also covers a reproduced nonfatal live stall:
successful playlists advance to a new continuity outside the current buffer,
while decoded frames and playback time remain stopped for ten seconds. The
demo restarts loading at the fresh live position through hls.js's public API.
Actual rolling-playlist tests retain the failing control, recovered video,
cancelled held requests and a ten-second no-progress failure. This does not
establish the cause of the older hosted MSE append error.

For an established live main playlist, the demo extends HTTP 502/503/504
retries within one fixed 60-second window from the first eligible failure;
the 32nd eligible failure refuses another retry. Quality changes do not renew the window;
a successful playlist update does. Scheduled extended retries are checked
again before dispatch, so hiding or replacing the player, or reaching the
deadline, prevents new retry I/O. Startup, VOD, other HTTP errors, request
timeouts, fragments and keys retain their original policies. Permanent
outages can therefore take longer to become fatal. Fatal records, peer
deadlines, account allowances and upload consent remain unchanged.

The publisher supports exact local playlist identities for mixed codec and
frame-rate variants, alternate audio, fMP4 maps, complete low-latency parts and
warm delta playlists. Schema 1 remains valid for its original contexts.
Schema 2 binds the exact playlist, media type and encryption context rather
than relying on a player's filtered level number. Init maps and keys remain
on HTTP. A part-capable host explicitly enables `swarmParts`; the demo exposes
that choice through `mediaCapabilities.parts`. Its 500 ms part reserve is
specific to the tested one-second-part/three-second-hold-back configuration;
the library default remains 2,000 ms and measured HTTP latency can raise it.

AES-128 ciphertext publication requires `allowEncryptedMedia: true`. A
commitment binds the local key path and IV; it neither publishes the key to
peers nor grants rights to redistribute protected media. DRM/SAMPLE-AES,
subtitles, I-frame variants, remote/query-bearing publisher assets and cold
delta reconstruction remain unsupported. Preload hints do not authorise
incomplete bytes for peer delivery.

## Signing and discovery

An author can sign a short-lived commitment delegation scoped to a stream,
swarm, delegate, rendition/media types, parts and maximum size. The signing
server can then operate with the delegate secret and the signed authorisation
without retaining the author's secret. Clients enforce scope, expiry and the
host's current revocation view. They do not infer that an offline revocation
list proves the absence of a newer revocation.

Full signed NIP-53 advertisements use a separate addressable identifier and
link the persistent commitment authorisation. Live/ended updates carry an
explicit streaming URL, relays, start time and bounded expiry. They do not
change the stable commitment identity. Discovery can require host-pinned
authorisations; event-selected relays and ICE servers do not replace host
endpoint policy. `/stream.json` exposes the current signed advertisement.

## Admission and upload allowance

The demo issues short-lived swarm/key-bound tickets after a signed one-use
possession challenge. Issuance, challenges and verification have separate
bounds. Revocation and epoch rotation are authenticated operator actions;
browser admission is checked again before connections, signalling and media
uploads. The embedded relay refuses unadmitted presence and signals and has
both connection and aggregate message bounds. These controls constrain work
and participating keys; they do not establish unique people or make an open
ticket endpoint a subscription service. Proxy headers do not establish a
trusted client address.

The browser saves media reservations under an origin-wide Web Lock and
origin storage record. Reloads and concurrent tabs share spent bytes;
upload consent and signing keys are never saved. Blocked, corrupt or
unavailable storage disables contribution. Viewers may deliberately increase
or reset the allowance. The quota covers reserved media payload, including
interrupted sends, rather than complete connection traffic.

An optional private account ledger adds reservations shared across devices.
The example supports explicit Nostr sign-in and a host-supplied authenticated
website account. Linking requires both proofs, adds recorded spend and retains
the lower limit. Connection and account changes leave upload consent off;
grants and identities stay outside swarm traffic and receipts. See the
[account allowance guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/ACCOUNT-UPLOAD-BUDGET.md) for persistence, privacy,
failure behaviour and the remaining acceptance scope.

## Operations and recovery

Opt-in reports carry a temporary page report identifier and sequence alongside
numeric cumulative values. Retries are idempotent, older snapshots do not
double-count, and decreasing counters are rejected. Private bounded state
retains policy, origin counters and the latest reports across orderly restart.
Origin counters use a short write debounce; they are observations rather than
an exact crash-proof billing ledger. Retention limits apply after reopening.

Broadcaster publication and worker supervision use two permanent SQLite lease
inodes on supported local POSIX filesystems. A worker guardian owns encoder
and forwarder process groups. On parent termination it kills and waits for
those workers before releasing its lease. An independent dirty marker is
written before launch and cleared only after cleanup. A killed guardian or
host catastrophe leaves recovery closed for explicit operator inspection;
PID namespace guesses and timed stale-lock deletion are not used. Distributed
volumes and Windows private-state ACLs are unsupported. Node 22.13+ is required.

## Installed native client

The installable package supplies `relayswarm-native` and the
`relayswarm/native-client` API. An application supplies a trusted descriptor
with digest, size, swarm, relay endpoints, allowed seeders and an optional HTTPS
origin. A bounded HyperDHT/Noise attempt precedes automatic verified HTTP
fallback. Redirects are refused. Exact size and SHA-256 are checked before
bytes are returned or a new output file is published. Cancellation does not
start fallback, and existing output files are never replaced.

Connections require the expected Noise key and acknowledged handshake writes
within one connection deadline. Final completion checks the absolute transfer
deadline even when synchronous work delays an abort timer. Discovery accepts
valid presence within its configured age bound while encrypted signals retain
their shorter subscription window.

The receiver subscribes before announcing receive-only native presence, with
no held objects and `open: false`. A seeder coalesces live replies globally to
at most one per second, using one timer and no requester map; close cancels a
pending reply. Relay history is optional for ephemeral events. This public
readiness metadata links the temporary Nostr identity and native public key;
only an exact signed dial can grant a transfer.

This entry point requires installed Node; it is not a self-contained binary.
The original `native-poc.mjs` remains a separate two-peer proof, with its
original failure-reporting behaviour. Neither client is durable media storage.

---

Source: [docs/PRODUCTION-READINESS.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/PRODUCTION-READINESS.md)

# Production delivery requirements

This checklist tracks the production work requested on 13 October 2026. It
retains the full scope of the feature review. Implementation, automated tests,
publication, deployment and physical acceptance are separate requirements.
An entry remains open until the evidence described below exists.

## Current deployed pilot: 21 October 2026

Exact `140c256` (PR 9) passed all nine required CI jobs, fresh 286-member
consumption of the committed source, guarded deployment with independent
review, P05 reporting acceptance (natural expiry after 303,923 ms) and P07
parent-crash recovery with an independent native review. The fourteen-role
short qualifier R66 is GREEN, 16 of 16 gates, the first green fourteen-role
qualifier, though it passed `each4BothQualityPeer` by one high-quality peer
segment. PR 9 merged as `1d54538`, published as experimental prerelease v0.2.1
and deployed through the guarded cycle with its own independent review: the
pilot app is `ce410033`, the served client is 787,462 bytes, and reporting and
forwarding remain off.

Several items are RED. v0.2.1's own short qualifier R68 is RED, 15 of 16 gates:
receivers switching to high quality received no high-quality peer segment, a
product mechanism on a one-segment margin (see
[current status](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md#current-delivery-checkpoint)). The sustained 7,200 s
run (Item 5) has not completed and is stopped by decision: R37 and R38 failed
on harness faults with no product evidence either way, and on `1d54538` it
cannot start without a matching qualifier. The P06 3 MB both-quality shared-cap lifecycle failed
again as in the a416f7e third run: three accepted 720p reservations were
charged but none completed as verified peer media over the relay path before
the fourth was refused as exhausted. It is a design limitation under relay
throughput, one high-quality holder and a 3 MB cap, with the allowance behaving
as documented. Desktop Firefox 152.0.6 and Safari 26.6.2 passed their journeys
(macOS arm64 desktop scope only); Safari 17.6 is RED with the cause not
determined. Physical devices, hard NAT, a separate network and marginal cost on
the hosts' plans remain open. See
[current status](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md#current-delivery-checkpoint), the
[checkpoint record](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/spikes/results/140c256-current-delivery-checkpoint-20261021.json)
and the [delivery checklist](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/PRODUCTION-READINESS.md#delivery-checklist).

## Previous deployed pilot: 19 October 2026

Exact `3f706a9` passed all nine required CI jobs, fresh 280-member consumption,
guarded HTTPS deployment and independent verification-source cleanup. The
browser client remains 773,458 bytes. Nostr accounts are enabled; the
authenticated host-supplied account API is implemented, with no website
resolver configured. Reporting and forwarding remain off.

P05 durable reporting acceptance now passes: trusted opt-in, duplicate
idempotence, same-volume restart persistence and natural expiry after
304.105 seconds. Reporting-off restoration and full browser/source cleanup
also passed independent review.

P07 crash acceptance remains RED. The latest test passed the parent-only
crash, strict writer audit, guarded marker recovery and server restart, while
preserving the original restart policy and permanent leases. The browser
exhausted its playlist retry budget on HTTP 502 responses before the server
returned; post-restart playback was not proved. An unchanged-source browser
regression also reproduces stopped playback after a 35-second HTTP 503 outage.
Browser and finite-source cleanup passed, and the acceptance window was not
extended. Retry and origin-only reconfiguration corrections are being verified;
see the [recovery checkpoint](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/spikes/results/3f706a9-parent-crash-recovery-checkpoint-20261019.json).

The matching fourteen-viewer qualifier remains unproved, so the two-hour run
is still ineligible. Both-quality shared-budget lifecycle, device/network

## Evidence rules

The existing pilot is a useful deployment starting point. A waiting page or a
running encoder does not prove media playback. Emulator and loopback receipts
do not prove physical-device or difficult-NAT behaviour. Peer media bytes are
not net wire-data or financial savings. A NIP draft and related codebase are
not proof of external standards acceptance or protocol interoperability.

Record the exact source, browser/device, topology, measurement window and
receipt path for each acceptance result. Preserve failing results until their
cause and regression are established. A completed duration can still fail its
acceptance gate. Connection counts do not establish accepted media payload.
Temporary-policy diagnostics do not establish default-device behaviour.
Update this table as evidence arrives; do not mark the overall work complete
while a required entry remains open.

---

Source: [docs/REALTIME-TRANSPORT.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/REALTIME-TRANSPORT.md)

# Experimental real-time transport

The source-only `relayswarm/realtime-peer` export carries opaque datagrams
over an explicitly selected WebRTC peer. It reuses `RelaySwarmSession` wire
version 3's signed pairwise NIP-44 signalling with a separate `webrtc-live`
transport token. HLS `PeerLink` and the loader keep their ordered reliable
protocol unchanged. This module is not included in the immutable v0.2.1
release or its browser bundle.

This is a transport component for a new call adapter, not an SFU, codec,
media-key service or room implementation. The application must authenticate
and encrypt media before sending it, authorise recipients, reassemble bounded
fragments, enforce frame deadlines and request video recovery after loss.
DTLS protects each link but does not by itself hide media from a forwarder
which terminates that link. No logging, recording, discovery announcement,
credential issuer or automatic peer/service selection is added here.

## API

```js
import { RealtimePeer } from 'relayswarm/realtime-peer';

// pool and session are host-selected and connected/started already.
// Resolve the selected peer's key through the application's trust policy.
const peer = new RealtimePeer({
  session,
  peerPubkey: selectedPeerPubkey,
  initiator: true,
  iceServers: deviceSelectedIceServers,
  iceTransportPolicy: 'relay',
  onDatagram: bytes => admitToBoundedFrameReceiver(bytes),
  onClose: reason => handleTransportClosure(reason),
  signal: cancellation.signal,
});
await peer.start(); // also available as peer.ready
const sent = peer.send(alreadyEncryptedFragment, {
  deadlineMs: performance.now() + 100,
});
if (!sent) requestApplicationRecovery();
// Bounded counters and generic states; no SDP, addresses, credentials or payloads.
const counters = peer.snapshot();
peer.close();
```

Construct the receiving side with `initiator: false` and its explicit sender
key, then start it before the initiator. Both sides can be given the same
`requestId` (8 to 64 URL-safe ASCII characters) when the host already has a
fresh negotiation capability. Otherwise the initiator generates a random ID
and the receiver binds to the first offer from its pinned peer. Replacement
uses a new peer instance. Caller admission remains necessary: knowing a
Nostr public key is not proof of room entitlement.

`start()` returns the same `ready` promise, resolving with its
`RealtimeDatagramLink`. The native connection is available as `peer.pc` for
caller read-only statistics. `send(Uint8Array | ArrayBuffer, { deadlineMs })`
returns a boolean. `deadlineMs` uses the same monotonic millisecond clock as
the optional injected `now()` callback; omitted deadlines have no transport
expiry. Once SCTP accepts bytes, the application cannot recall them. A
receiver must still reject an expired complete frame.

`RealtimeDatagramLink` can wrap an application-negotiated `pc`/`channel`
directly. It requires the label `relayswarm-live-v1` and `ordered: false`.
The default mode requires `maxRetransmits: 0` and `maxPacketLifeTime: null`.
An explicit `maxPacketLifeTimeMs` option (integer 1 to 1000) instead requires
`maxRetransmits: null` and exactly the selected `maxPacketLifeTime` value.
Both endpoints must select the same mode and lifetime. Ordered, reliable,
different-lifetime and different-mode channels are refused; there is no
automatic switch or HLS fallback. The same constraints apply to channels
received by `RealtimePeer`. Snapshots name the selected delivery mode and
lifetime without exposing credentials or payloads.

Peer snapshots also retain a generic close reason, current/pre-close native
connection/ICE/gathering/signalling/channel states, candidate counts and
description-presence booleans. The pre-close state remains available after
the underlying connection has been closed. These are in-memory observations
on explicit request; no logger or history writer is added.

For a media forwarding service, explicitly selecting 50 ms lifetime bounds
unsent and retransmission eligibility in a correctly implemented backend.
Zero retries alone does not impose an unsent queue deadline. Negotiated flags
do not prove backend conformance; use the guarded Node correction below.

## Bounds and lifetime

- Default datagrams are at most 16 KiB; the configurable hard maximum is
  64 KiB. Larger media frames need application fragmentation.
- Default SCTP buffered-data allowance is 256 KiB, configurable up to 4 MiB.
  A send that would exceed the allowance is dropped, without an application
  transport queue, retry or deferred send.
- Async receive callbacks are capped at 16 in flight by default on the link.
  Additional datagrams are dropped; callback rejection closes with a generic
  reason. A synchronous admission callback can hand bytes to a separately
  bounded receiver. Closing cannot cancel an already-running callback, so
  callers must check their own cancellation before applying async results.
- Each peer accepts at most 128 ICE candidates per direction, at most 4 KiB
  per candidate and 6 KiB SDP. Candidate-before-description and replica
  reordering are retained only inside those bounds. The default connection
  deadline is 15 seconds (configurable up to 60 seconds).
- Abort, timeout, native/channel failure or explicit close removes listeners,
  clears candidate queues, closes channel/connection and rejects unfinished
  readiness with a generic error. The caller owns the shared session/pool;
  closing one peer does not close those shared resources.
- `iceServers` and `iceTransportPolicy` are supplied by the host. The policy
  defaults to `relay` with no ICE servers. No root TURN secret or default
  service is supplied. An empty relay configuration cannot establish a path.

## Verification scope

Run `npm run test:realtime`. The tests exercise bounds, late data, protocol
refusal, cancellation, timeout, pinned peers/IDs, candidate reordering and an
actual `RelayPool`/NIP-44 session exchange through an in-memory relay. The
native peer connection in these unit tests is a fixture, so they do not prove
browser SCTP behaviour, WAN/NAT traversal, real media playback or a complete
Spry/Sapflow/KithMoot call. Those require the consuming adapter's integration
tests. This component establishes no legal exemption for the combined offering.

`npm run test:realtime:native` additionally runs an actual Chromium initiator
against a Node werift 0.24.3 answerer, with real WebRTC and encrypted session
signalling over a loopback relay. Both directions carry generated datagrams
and the native incoming channel must be unordered with zero retransmits.
The qualifier requires the matching Playwright Chromium installation (or
`E2E_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE`). It passed on the development Mac. It does not
exercise TURN, remote networks, audiovisual decoding or phone devices.

The original uncorrected Node qualifier role is **answerer only**. Werift 0.24.3's outgoing DCEP
encoding overwrites the unordered channel bit when maxRetransmits is set;
an initiating werift peer therefore fails the strict receiver check. Do not
weaken that check to make a Node initiator pass. The browser initiates each
connection to an independent Node forwarding operator. The receiver accepts
the browser's correctly encoded unordered channel and sends on that channel.

Always pass explicit ICE configuration to the Node implementation. Werift
otherwise supplies a default STUN service; it selects the first supplied
STUN and TURN URL rather than establishing browser-like multi-server
fallback. Source inspection maps relay policy to its `forceTurn` option;
that inspection is not a live TURN qualification. Operator wrappers must
also disable/reject inherited dependency debugging (`DEBUG`) before opening
connections: dependency diagnostics can include ICE credentials. The
transport module itself adds no logger.

## Guarded Node backend build

The opt-in `relayswarm/realtime-werift-build` module corrects one exact
werift 0.24.4 ESM source revision during an esbuild Node build. It neither
edits installed packages nor changes another application's dependency.
The exported `weriftRealtimeRevision` records the reviewed upstream file
SHA-256 values. Unknown metadata/source, browser builds, external-package
builds and unsupported werift subpath imports are refused. There is no
uncorrected fallback.

```js
import { build } from 'esbuild';
import { realtimeWeriftPlugin } from 'relayswarm/realtime-werift-build';

await build({
  entryPoints: ['operator-entry.mjs'], // imports RTCPeerConnection from werift
  outfile: 'operator.mjs',
  platform: 'node', format: 'esm', bundle: true,
  // Supply the normal createRequire shim if bundled dependencies require it.
  plugins: [await realtimeWeriftPlugin({ packageRoot: reviewedWeriftDirectory })],
});
```

The changes preserve unordered DCEP mode bits, recognise zero retransmits,
capture lifetime in monotonic seconds when the data-channel send is enqueued, discard
expired application-queue data, and refuse expired SCTP data before first
send or retransmission. A single timer per association expires queued media
even without a window-opening event. Abandonment identifies the exact DATA
chunk and its message fragments rather than another message with the same
chunk type. Flight-byte accounting follows abandonment and retransmission.
The latest FORWARD TSN control skip is retained until cumulative acknowledgement
and retried using the unchanged control timer if lost; expired media is not
retransmitted. Association closure cancels its added expiry timer.
The upstream MIT notice is retained explicitly in the generated bundle,
alongside dependency legal comments. The published npm package omitted its
licence file; the notice comes from the
[upstream repository licence](https://github.com/shinyoshiaki/werift-webrtc/blob/develop/LICENSE).
The guard does not independently pin all transitive dependencies: retain the
consuming application's lockfile and build provenance as separate inputs.

Correction revision 2 also releases a successfully allocated TURN lease on
shutdown. It aborts the scheduled positive refresher, settles outstanding
transactions, sends authenticated Refresh with lifetime zero to the already
resolved server, handles stale nonce with fresh transaction IDs, then closes
the socket in all outcomes. Up to three attempts share a 900 ms release
budget; a server which cannot acknowledge release still owns allocation
expiry. Closing is idempotent. Peer/server requests cannot resume after close
and register another transaction after asynchronous address resolution.
Failed allocation also closes its newly created transport. These corrections
do not increase server quotas or replace them with fresh-credential churn.

Run the conformance tests with the reviewed installation supplied explicitly:

```sh
WERIFT_REALTIME_PACKAGE_ROOT=/path/to/reviewed/node_modules/werift npm run test:realtime:backend
```

Without that variable the conformance command fails; it cannot turn green
by skipping the backend cases. With the reviewed source, the tests build the
corrected module and exercise actual serialised SCTP packets through a finite
in-memory lossy transport. They prove zero-retry loss recovery, expiry behind
a zero receive window, correct message selection, fragmented-message loss
and lifetime-unit/application-queue handling. They also cover wall-clock
rollback, lost control-skip recovery and expiry timer cleanup. The packet fixture accelerates
the retransmission trigger; production retry timers, ICE consent and native
resource limits remain unchanged. This is SCTP wire proof, not WAN or physical
device qualification.

The same suite additionally runs the actual corrected TURN client against
an authenticated loopback UDP fixture. It verifies nonce/authenticated release,
lost requests, an unresponsive server, refresher/request cancellation, failed
allocation and two successive batches of eight sockets reusing one credential
under an eight-allocation limit. These control-plane tests do not replace
the consuming application's public-server allocation/readback gate.

The Chromium-to-native qualifier can consume the generated module explicitly:

```sh
E2E_REALTIME_BACKEND_MODULE=/path/to/corrected-backend.mjs E2E_REALTIME_LIFETIME_MS=50 npm run test:realtime:native
```

That path is a mandatory explicit selection when qualifying finite-lifetime
native forwarding. An omitted backend path retains the historical direct
upstream diagnostic; it does not establish corrected loss/expiry behaviour.

---

Source: [docs/TRANSFER-WORKER.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/TRANSFER-WORKER.md)

# Dedicated transfer worker

This unreleased experimental opt-in moves schema-3 piece verification and
transfer scheduling into one dedicated worker per swarm, for mixed and
explicit peer-only transfers. Both execution paths
share the same small transfer facade and compiled Rust module. Piece hashes,
the whole-object hash, planner, probe caps and returned commands remain Rust's
decisions; there is no additional JavaScript verifier.

## Host integration and packaging

Bundle the companion entry from the same SDK revision as the main adapter and
reviewed WASM module. From this repository, using its installed dependencies:

```sh
npx --no-install esbuild src/browser/core-transfer-worker-runtime.mjs --bundle --platform=browser --format=esm --outfile=public/relayswarm-transfer-worker.mjs
```

Serve that generated file and configure its URL explicitly:

```js
const swarm = createHlsSwarm({
  ...approvedStreamOptions,
  mode: "peer-first",
  coreWasm: "/vendor/relayswarm-core.wasm",
  multiHolder: true,
  transferWorkerUrl: "/relayswarm-transfer-worker.mjs",
});
swarm.attach(hls);
```

`transferWorkerUrl` requires peer-first mode, `coreWasm` and `multiHolder`.
The host's normal explicit peer/upload consent still applies. A relative
`import.meta.url` inside a bundled main library does not guess an adjacent
asset. Existing browser worker/module capabilities and the host's content
policy must permit the supplied URL; refusal goes to HTTP. Installed-package
bundlers can resolve the entry as `relayswarm/transfer-worker`, for example
from a companion entry containing `import "relayswarm/transfer-worker"`.
The SDK release build emits `relayswarm-transfer-worker-VERSION.mjs` with
metadata and a checksum alongside the browser bundle. Existing
immutable release downloads do not contain this unreleased feature.

`loadCore(...)` exposes its already compiled `module`, a
`WebAssembly.Module`. The swarm warms the worker asynchronously from that
module, without a second WASM fetch or holding session/player startup. While
the worker is warming or after a worker failure, configured peer-first loads
use ordinary HTTP before any metadata or coordinated wait. They do not quietly
retry a large Rust transfer on the main thread. The synchronous/native transfer
API and unconfigured swarms retain their existing path. Once the worker is
ready, schemas 1/2 retain their existing path too.

The companion imports only the shared transfer facade. It receives a cloned
compiled module, numeric scheduler inputs, commitment digests and media bytes.
Native peer connections and signalling keys remain in the main host. It
performs no media fetch, creates no peer connection and selects no player.

## Bounds, cancellation and observations

The default bridge permits two active objects, 16 MiB per object, 32 MiB of
active object sizes, 32 pending calls and 32 MiB of pending media payload.
The loader respects its configured segment limit up to the bridge's 32 MiB
per-object maximum. Initialisation and every call have a five-second safety
deadline; the existing HLS peer floor and absolute origin backstop remain in
force independently. Queue or handle exhaustion sends that load to HTTP.
There is no automatic worker retry or unbounded queue.

Media input is copied into an owned transferable buffer so the caller retains
its original bytes for caching, accounting and tracing. Verified output is
transferred back. This moves CPU work and retains an input-copy cost; it does
not prove lower total CPU time or network use.

Per-transfer free/cancel immediately fences its replies, rejects pending
calls and queues Rust handle cleanup; other active transfers continue.
Acknowledgements or operation deadlines still own that queued work, because
only terminating the worker can interrupt a synchronous WASM call. Swarm
stop, worker failure, malformed results or a genuine operation deadline
terminate the worker and reject pending work. The normal pending HTTP arm of
a cached-peer race remains owned by its loader.

The loader keeps generation/abort guards and complete-object acceptance.
An explicit clock check fences worker replies at the absolute backstop even
when its timer has not run; the mixed path retains its origin reserve.
Late worker replies cannot credit peer bytes or call the player. Only
first-verified-copy contributions in an accepted complete object reach
`onPeerDelivery`. `metrics().core.transferWorker` reports state/reason and,
once available, active objects, pending calls and pending media bytes. It
contains no native connection references.

The low-level [`createCoreTransferWorker`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/src/browser/core-transfer-worker.mjs)
bridge also accepts a compiled `module` and explicit `workerUrl`, with bounded
limits, a lifecycle `signal` and `onFailure`. Its `transfer(config, { signal })`
returns asynchronous `start`, `progress`, `delivered`, `failed` and `tick`
methods with the synchronous core's arguments and frames. `free`/`cancel`
release one handle; `stop` terminates the worker. `WorkerImpl` on the HLS
options is a constructor injection point for tests or an equivalent host
worker transport.

## Explicit peer-only cached race

When no safe serial wait remains, `zeroBudgetPeerRace` starts one normal
whole-object HTTP request immediately. The competing Rust transfer is created
with `peerOnly: true`: there is no origin lane, origin estimate or ignored
origin command inside it. Fast whole-HTTP history cannot strand ranges behind
work that performs no I/O. Candidate identity stays inside the initial cached
snapshot and current HAVE by default.

Cold holders receive bounded one-piece calibration. Remaining unverified,
uncovered pieces stay pending until verified progress refills bounded peer
requests. Failed or corrupt holders return only unfinished work to that pool.
No speculative serial-recovery abandonment kills this already-parallel arm;
the real HTTP winner, peer floor and host cancellation own its lifetime.
At the floor, Rust cancels peers and fails this transfer while normal HTTP
continues. Piece and whole-object hashes, request size, holder, worker queue
and upload allowance bounds remain in force. Normal mixed transfers retain
their origin lane and existing abandonment rules.

The optional capability mask is `2` (alongside bounded-probe mask `1`).
Low-level callers request `peerOnly: true` in transfer creation, then supply
`origin: null` at start. Existing constructor/C/native signatures remain
compatible. A synchronous core without the capability declines before
allocation; a worker declines that handle without retiring healthy mixed
transfers. HLS retains its already-running HTTP arm. No synthetic origin
latency is substituted.

Ranged requests are charged by their actual bounded size under unchanged
rate and session limits. Unlike a whole-object upload, an entire large media
object need not fit one two-second rate bucket. The temporary whole-object
fallback was hash-safe but lost the same-M4 native first-load comparison;
that failed control is retained. New mode qualification still requires the
unchanged native three-load win/HTTP-win/win assertion and physical playback
evidence; the capability alone is not a performance guarantee.

### Optional late HAVE

With `zeroBudgetPeerRace` and the separate experimental `lateHaveRace: true`,
an already-running whole HTTP load can race an object advertised later on a
connection accepted at load entry. This uses the existing key-filtered HAVE
notifications. FETCH is not cached data; no neighbour search or new connection
is admitted. The first actual matching holder snapshot is frozen once, and
failure or corruption does not start a second arm.

Key hashing, HAVE observation, commitment verification and peer delivery all
consume the same original `maxPeerWaitMs` window. HTTP never waits and no
origin range is created. Its success or exposed progressive chunk cancels
the observation and worker handle; swarm stop preserves pending normal HTTP,
while loader abort or destroy cancels both arms. Upload and worker bounds
remain unchanged. The zero-budget `have-after-wait` diagnostic marks a real
later HAVE, not deferred HTTP. A peer winner can still leave partial HTTP
traffic; the host must measure that traffic before claiming network savings.

## Focused verification

```sh
node --test test/core-transfer-worker.test.mjs test/core-transfer.test.mjs
node --test --test-name-pattern='transfer worker:' test/browser-hardening.test.mjs
node --test --test-name-pattern='^late-HAVE race' test/browser-hardening-core.mjs
```

The bridge fixture uses a real Node worker thread with the committed WASM,
comparing every six-MiB mixed/corrupt transfer frame and final bytes against
the synchronous core. It covers independent cleanup, limits, stale replies,
deadlines, worker errors and stop. Loader checks cover a six-MiB verified
contribution with exact observations, HTTP during held initialisation with a
real FETCH/no HAVE, delayed replies within and past the origin reserve,
ordinary HTTP surviving peer shutdown, and genuine worker failure with no
peer credit or synchronous retry. These
are protocol/lifecycle checks; physical HLS continuity and net network benefit
remain separate acceptance gates.
